activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In 1868 the Senate acquitted President Andrew Johnson by one vote: 35 senators voted to convict, one short of the two-thirds needed.
story:
The courthouse steps were still warm from the afternoon when Emile unfolded the debate brief Mr. Crowchild had photocopied for all three of them, and the wind immediately tried to take it. Talha grabbed a corner. Isabela stood with her back to the door, timing them on her phone, because the regional finals were inside in forty minutes and the judges did not wait for anyone.

"Draw for sides," Talha said. "Winner picks."

Emile won and picked the argument that a presidential system sets the bar for removing a head of government too high. It was the harder side, which was why he wanted it. Isabela would defend the two-thirds requirement, and she had been preparing all week, which he knew because she'd stopped sitting with them at lunch and started carrying a binder with tabs.

Inside, in the marble hallway where the public trials were posted on a corkboard, they ran the first exchange. Isabela moved smoothly through the parliamentary case: a prime minister who loses the confidence of the house can fall in a single afternoon, by a simple majority, and the machine keeps running with a new head of government the same week. "That's responsiveness," she said. "That's the system protecting itself."

"Or eating itself," Emile said. "A bare majority can decapitate the government every time it gets annoyed. Stability has a value too." But he could feel the argument sliding sideways on him, because the presidential side needed proof that the high bar did actual harm, and the American example he kept reaching for had ended, historically, without a removal. He had the shape of a fact in his head and could not find its edges.

"Twenty minutes," Isabela said.

Mr. Crowchild came down the hallway with a paper cup of coffee and, unasked, handed Emile the courthouse's small display case key. "While you're waiting, the exhibit room's open. Some of you might find the wall on the impeachment trials more interesting than this hallway." He said it mildly and walked on, and Emile understood he was being handed something, though not what.

The exhibit room was cold and smelled like floor wax. One wall held enlarged facsimiles of Senate documents, and Talha read faster than him, which was unfair. "Here," Talha said, tapping the glass. "In 1868 the Senate acquitted President Andrew Johnson by one vote. Thirty-five senators voted to convict, one short of the two-thirds needed."

Emile stood in front of the number for a long moment. One vote. A president one senator away from removal, and the bar held. He tried to internalize it, turn it from a fact on a wall into something he could hold up in an argument, but it kept doubling on him. It proved his point and broke it at the same time: the bar was so high that even thirty-five conviction votes were not enough, and yet a country that had survived a civil war had also survived that acquittal. In a parliamentary system, Johnson would have been gone in a week, replaced quietly, like a fuse. Whether that fuse was a safety feature or a weakness was exactly the thing he could not settle, standing there in the cold room, and he suspected the judges couldn't either.

"Emile," Talha said. "Eight minutes."

They went back out. In the hallway Isabela was talking to a woman from another school about the parliamentary question, quick and fluent, and when Emile told her what the wall said, her face changed. She hadn't known the number either. "So he survived by one vote," she said slowly. "One."

"That's the whole fight," Emile said. "You're going to say the system held. I'm going to say a system that needs thirty-five senators and still can't act is a system that decided, in advance, that it almost never will."

"And what will you say when I ask what the alternative costs?"

He didn't have it yet. The numbered doors along the hallway opened and closed; a clerk called a case name; somewhere a jury was being seated, ordinary people deciding a man's future by a standard Emile suddenly wanted to interrogate. "I'll say I'm not sure," he told her. "And then I'll argue it anyway."

Isabela checked her phone, then held the courtroom door open. "Two minutes. You go first."

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: China's campaign to kill sparrows, launched in 1958, removed a predator of crop-eating insects, and locust swarms that followed contributed to the Great Chinese Famine.
story:
Jacob had forty-one dollars in his pocket and a petition with ninety-three signatures, and neither was going to be enough.

The library meeting room smelled like burnt coffee and old carpet. The community garden had been losing seedlings all spring, and tonight the gardeners would vote on a proposal to clear the nesting boxes out of the oak by the fence, the ones the town had installed three years ago with a small grant and a ribbon-cutting nobody remembered anymore. Rory's mother, who kept the plot beside the compost bins, had drafted the proposal. Rory sat at the folding table with the clipboard, half embarrassed, half loyal.

"Every sprout I put in, they pull out," she said to the room. "We net the beds, they go under the net. We feed the neighborhood and we're feeding sparrows instead."

Jacob hadn't come to speak. He'd come because he'd spent the last month in the stacks upstairs researching a history paper, and somewhere between the microfilm machine and the yellow bound volumes of agricultural reports, he had found a paragraph that kept following him home. He'd copied it onto an index card, then copied it again when the first card got soft from handling.

The vote was called. Mr. Asante, who ran the Saturday seed swap and had a voice that carried without being raised, stood up first. "Before we decide, I'd like to hear from anybody who's done some looking into it. Anybody at all."

The room was quiet. A radiator ticked. Jacob's heart did something complicated, the kind of thing that both exhilarated and terrified him, and he stood up before he could think better of it.

"In 1958, China launched a campaign to kill sparrows," he said, and heard how strange it sounded, a sixteen-year-old in a library basement talking about a country that no longer existed in that form. "Everyone thought sparrows were eating the crops, so they went after them. But sparrows also eat crop-eating insects. The locust swarms that followed contributed to the Great Chinese Famine." He held up the index card as if it were evidence at a trial, which, in a way, it was. "I'm not saying our sparrows are the same. I'm saying when you take a piece out because it's inconvenient, you don't always know what it was holding up."

"That's China," Rory's mother said. "This is a garden."

"That's fair," Jacob said, and meant it. He had thought about this the night before, walking home under the sodium lights, turning the problem over the way you turn a stone to see the damp underneath. "A garden isn't a country. But it's not just a garden either. It sits on the flood line, the runoff from the parking lot comes through it, the food bank takes what we grow. It's all connected whether we planned it that way or not. Remove the birds, maybe the beetles take over. Maybe nothing happens and the sprouts survive. I honestly don't know."

Rory was watching him with an expression he couldn't read. They had been friends since the summer program where they'd built the compost bins, and he knew she agreed with her mother about the sparrows, and he knew she also knew the food bank numbers, which had gone up two Octobers in a row.

"That's not a reason to do nothing," someone said from the back. "That's a reason to do anything."

"It's a reason to do the small thing first," Mr. Asante said. "Row covers. Reflective tape. Try the plot level before the fence line level."

Rory's mother called that specious, a word Jacob had to look up later on his phone, tapping it in while the vote was counted, and when he saw the definition he understood she meant it sounded reasonable while being empty. But her voice wavered, and when the hands went up, the proposal failed by four votes. She gathered her clipboard and left through the fire door, and Rory stayed, which Jacob knew would cost her something at home.

Afterward, Mr. Asante shook his hand and said, "You did your work. That's all anybody can do," and then he said the thing Jacob would think about for weeks, walking past the garden on his way to school. "The confounder in any decision like this is time. You won't know if you were right until long after it stops mattering whether you were."

That night, Jacob sat at the kitchen table drafting a message to Rory, deleting and rewriting, because she hadn't spoken to him since the vote and the blue checkmarks under his last attempt sat there unanswered.

"I'm not sure I was right," he wrote finally. "I only know we'd have been more wrong to guess in the other direction. Meet me Saturday at the seed swap? We can put up the row covers together. I'll bring the tape."

He watched the screen. Outside, the oak along the fence was just a shape in the dark, holding whatever it was holding, and then three dots appeared under his message, blinking on and off like something small deciding whether to land.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: In England and Wales, a landlord must place a tenant's deposit in a government-backed protection scheme within 30 days of receiving it.
story:
Natalie had the appointment at half past four on a Thursday, wedged between her shift at the bakery and the bus home, because she had decided that the summer before university was the summer she would learn to be an adult about money. The real estate office smelled of instant coffee and carpet shampoo, and a woman behind the desk with a dour expression was telling a man that the flat he wanted had already gone, that flats went fast, that he ought to have moved quicker. Natalie sat in the waiting area with her hands folded and rehearsed her questions.

"Miss Okafor?" A man in a blue tie, not Mr. Siddiqui but a younger agent, beckoned her into a glass-walled office. She had met Mr. Siddiqui once, at the community meeting about the new development, and he had told her to come in if she ever wanted to understand how any of it worked. The younger agent had clearly been told the same thing.

"So," he said. "You're looking to rent?"

"I'm seventeen," Natalie said. "I'm looking to understand. My mum pays rent and I never see where it goes. I want to know how it works before I have to do it."

He leaned back, seemed to decide this was a legitimate use of his afternoon, and pulled a sheet of paper toward him. He drew a line down it. On the left he wrote the monthly rent, the deposit, the referencing fee. On the right he started a different set of numbers and explained that renting was paying for the use of somewhere without owning it, while a mortgage was a loan you took to buy, paid back over decades with interest, and that the bank wanted a down payment first, a chunk of the price in cash, usually a serious chunk, before it would lend you the rest.

"So the deposit on a rental," Natalie said, "is not the same thing at all."

"Different animal entirely," he said. "The rental deposit is security. It's the landlord's cushion if you damage the place or leave owing rent. It's still your money, in principle. You're supposed to get it back."

"In principle," Natalie repeated, and wrote it down, because that phrase felt like a crack in the floor she should look through. She asked what happened to the money while the tenant lived there, where it actually sat, and he said that depended on where you were, and started explaining the local rules, and she thought of Ryann.

Ryann had moved to Manchester in September, into a house share with four other students, and last week he had messaged their group chat a screenshot of a bank transfer and a question that no one had answered: does anyone else think it's weird that I never got any paperwork about my deposit? The chat had moved on to someone's birthday plans, and Ryann's question had sunk beneath them, but Natalie had kept thinking about it, the way a worry can metastasize in a group chat, small and unanswered until it feels enormous in private.

She asked the agent, choosing her words carefully, whether the rules were different in England, because she had a friend there, a student, who paid a deposit months ago and had received nothing since. The agent turned to his screen, typed, and read for a while, and Natalie watched his finger move down the page.

"There's a scheme over there," he said. "A landlord must put the tenant's deposit in a government-backed protection scheme within 30 days of receiving it. That's the rule in England and Wales. Your friend should have had something about it by now, paperwork, details of the scheme. If he's had nothing, that's not normal."

"So it's not normal," Natalie said, and felt the strange satisfaction of a suspicion confirmed, which was also the strange dread of a suspicion confirmed.

She left with the sheet of paper folded in her pocket and the agent's card, and she walked to the bus stop and messaged Ryann while the streetlights came on: ask your landlord which scheme your deposit is in, they had to put it in a government-backed protection scheme within 30 days of getting it, and you should have had paperwork. Then she added, ask him for it in writing. Ryann replied with three messages of disbelief and one of gratitude, and then, ten minutes later, with a photograph of an email from his letting agent, apologising, attaching a certificate, dated that afternoon.

It was the following Tuesday that the reversal arrived. Natalie had gone back to the office to return the pen she had accidentally walked out with, a small errand she had dressed up as a follow-up question about mortgage rates, and Mr. Siddiqui himself was at the front desk, sorting keys into labelled drawers. He recognised her, asked how her research was going, and she told him about Ryann, about the 30 days and the protection scheme, laying it out with the fluency of someone who had explained it twice already.

"Good lad, whoever told you that," Mr. Siddiqui said, and then he laughed, a short dry sound, and shook his head at the drawer of keys. "I've owned this building twenty years. I let the flat upstairs myself, cash in hand, no scheme, no paperwork, nothing. My tenant's been asking for her certificate for two months." He slid the drawer shut and picked up his phone. "I'd better go make a call."

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: The US Fair Labor Standards Act took effect on October 24, 1938, setting the first federal minimum wage at 25 cents an hour and a maximum workweek of 44 hours.
story:
Riley clocked in at four and found the schedule taped to the break room door, his hours cut again, eleven this week when the union contract promised a floor of fifteen. Kaiya was already there, arms crossed, reading it like a verdict. "They can't do this," she said. "The contract says fifteen hours minimum for anyone past ninety days. I'm past ninety days, you're past ninety days."

The store was doing its slow midweek undulate of carts down the aisles, one customer drifting behind another. Riley restocked cereal while he thought about it. He needed the hours for tuition deposits due in August, but he also needed not to get fired two months before he left for college, and those two needs did not point the same direction. "Maybe I just talk to Ms. Kim," he said when Kaiya found him in the aisle. "Quietly."

"Or," Kaiya said, "we file a grievance, which is what the contract is for. My dad lost a job once for asking for overtime he'd earned. I'm not doing the quiet thing." She was already pulling the steward's number off the union board by the timeclock, the number nobody ever called.

Ishaan, who worked the register and treated every workplace dispute as a spectator sport, was facetious about it at first. "Comrade Kaiya leads the revolution from aisle seven," he announced during his break, but then he lowered his voice. "Seriously, though, I looked some of this up after they cut my hours in March. Did you know the first federal minimum wage in this country was twenty-five cents an hour?"

"No," Riley said.

"October 24, 1938. The Fair Labor Standards Act. And the max workweek it set back then was forty-four hours." Ishaan shrugged, embarrassed by his own knowledge. "I found it because I was mad, and then I kept reading, and honestly it made me madder and less mad at the same time. Twenty-five cents. But it was something. It was the first something."

Riley thought about that while he faced the cans, turning every label outward. He had always assumed the rules were just there, like gravity, and now he understood they had been argued into existence, hour by hour, by people whose names nobody remembered. At the same time he understood Ms. Kim, who had explained once, tired, that the store's labor budget came from somewhere above her, from people who had never walked these aisles. Maybe she was cutting their hours because someone above her was cutting hers. That didn't make it legal, but it made her not exactly the enemy, and Riley held both of those ideas at once without managing to flatten either one.

Kaiya called the steward from the loading dock, and on Thursday a union rep named only by his first name came in, a heavyset man named Victor who bought a banana and stayed two hours. Riley watched him and Ms. Kim in the office through the little window in the door, papers passed back and forth, her hands flat on the desk, his leaning forward. When he left, he stopped by the registers. "Contract's clear," he said to Kaiya, loud enough for the aisle. "They'll restore the hours or pay the difference. That part's not complicated. Whether they try it again, that's the complicated part."

Ms. Kim called Riley into the office on Friday. She had his schedule in front of her, corrected, fifteen hours, and she slid it across the desk without ceremony. "I should have caught it," she said. "I didn't write the cuts, but I posted them, and posting them is the part I did." She looked at him for a moment. "You going to be one of those people who files things, Riley?" He said he didn't know yet, and it was true, and she nodded like that was an acceptable answer.

His last shift before college fell on a Saturday. The carts undulated bright down the aisles, and Ishaan was telling a new kid, a sixteen-year-old who was getting eight hours and hadn't thought to question it, about the twenty-five cents. "Twenty-five cents an hour," Ishaan said, waving a box of cereal like evidence. "And forty-four hours max, that was the whole workweek they set, back at the very beginning. So when Kaiya says fifteen hours is the floor here, she's standing on like ninety years of people griping until griping became a law."

Kaiya appeared at the end of the aisle with a clipboard, starting a petition for cross-training pay, something she wanted even though she'd be gone in a year herself. She looked at Riley. "You in or you out?" Riley took the pen, but before he signed he looked down the aisle, at the new kid listening, at Ms. Kim watching from the office window with an expression he couldn't read, at the schedule board where his fifteen hours sat in neat ink. He signed his name under Kaiya's. "Somebody named Victor should know," he said, and went to find the number.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Under the US Fair Labor Standards Act, non-exempt employees must be paid one and a half times their regular rate for hours worked beyond 40 in a workweek.
story:
The wind off the lake had a boreal edge to it even indoors, sliding under the natatorium doors every time a swimmer came through, and Camille had learned to keep her towel around her shoulders between rotations. She had wanted this job since she was eleven, since the summer a lifeguard had pulled her little brother out of the deep end at this same pool, and now, at sixteen, she sat in the tall white chair with the whistle between her teeth and watched the water fold and unfold. Over winter break she had picked up every shift nobody wanted, the six a.m. lap swims and the Sunday masters practices, partly because she liked the quiet of the pool at that hour and partly because her mother had mentioned, twice, without ever asking, the cost of her textbooks for the fall.

The schedule for the last week of break was taped to the door of the guard room, and under the grid of names Ms. Fischer had written a note in her small, square handwriting, the kind that looked like it had been decided on before it was written: Camille, you are at 44 hours this week. We will talk. Below it, the usual bromide from the corporate poster, SAFETY FIRST, which everyone ignored so completely that it had become invisible, like the drains at the bottom of the pool.

She didn't understand the number until her next paycheck. She sat on the folding table in the guard room with Finnley and Saad, all three of them still smelling of chlorine, and stared at the line where her pay rate jumped. Some of her hours had been paid at one and a half times her regular rate. "What is this," she said, and Saad leaned over, chewing the last of a granola bar, and said, "Overtime. Anything over forty hours in a workweek, they have to pay you time and a half. It's the law." Finnley said he'd heard of it but had never hit forty hours in his life, and Saad said he'd hit it once, at the garden center, and had watched his check climb like water rising in a lock.

Finnley watched Camille look at the number for a long moment, and he could see her doing the thing she did in calculus, working backward from an answer to the reasoning underneath it. He liked that about her, though he would never have said so out loud, because Saad would make it a whole thing. What he noticed now, and what she seemed not to, was that her jaw was set. He recognized the set of it. It was the same look she'd had when the coach benched her brother for a game he hadn't missed a practice for. He nudged the granola wrapper into the trash with his heel and said, "You're going to talk to Fischer."

"I'm going to ask her if she knew," Camille said. "Because if she didn't, then last week's check was wrong too, and so was Saad's, that week the garden center people called him in. And if she did know, then she scheduled me forty-four hours anyway, and that's a different conversation." Saad said, quietly, that plenty of places just, you know, quietly didn't, and Camille said, "They can't just abrogate it because it's inconvenient. It's not a suggestion." She folded the check and put it in the pocket of her parka, and the three of them went back out to the deck, where the afternoon light came low and blue through the tall windows.

She sent a message that night instead of cornering Ms. Fischer at the pool, because a cornered person defends and a messaged person can think. Ms. Fischer, she wrote, I checked my check and some of my hours were paid at a higher rate, time and a half, for hours over forty in the workweek. Was that right? Because if it was right, then I think my earlier checks were wrong, and Saad thinks his were too. I'm not trying to make trouble. I just want the number to be true. She read it four times before she sent it, and then she put the phone face down on her desk and did not sleep especially well.

The reply came at seven the next morning. Camille: thank you for writing instead of guessing, that was the right way to do this. You are correct about the rate. You were right last week as well and I have flagged it with payroll, and Saad's checks too, which I should have caught myself. The corrected amounts will appear within two pay periods. And Camille, I am sorry. I have been doing this for nineteen years and I still let a scheduling program make decisions I should have made myself. Come see me before your shift.

She went in an hour early, and Ms. Fischer had the schedule grid open on the desk, and she had already rewritten the last week of break. Camille's hours stopped at exactly forty. "I can't in good conscience keep scheduling you past forty every week," Ms. Fischer said, tapping the grid. "Not with the budget as it is. So I've split the extra shifts between Finnley and the new guard. You keep every hour you have, and you keep the raise I'm giving you, because a guard who checks her own numbers and writes to me like an adult is worth more to this pool than four overtime hours." She slid the paper across. "Head guard, effective spring. It pays better than overtime did."

Camille took the schedule and said thank you, and meant it, and walked out through the equipment room where the January air came knifing under the door, and stood for a moment with her hand on the cold steel of the door handle, doing the arithmetic she could not stop herself from doing. By asking, by being right, by being thanked and promoted for it, she had arranged things so that there would never again be a line on her paycheck at one and a half times anything. She had wanted the number to be true, and now it was true, and it was smaller. Saad was waiting by the lockers with two hot chocolates, one of them obviously for her, and he held it out and asked how it went.

"I got a raise," she said, and took the cup. "And I lost the overtime."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Concussion guidelines say an athlete with a suspected concussion should not return to play on the same day, even if they feel fine.
story:
The natatorium smelled of chlorine and the cold air that pooled around the doors in January, and Ryan had loved that smell for exactly one season, which was all the time he'd been on the water polo team. He had joined because Noam joined, and Noam had joined because the pool was warm in winter, and neither of them had expected to care. Now it was February, the league finals were in three weeks, and Ryan was treading water at the six-meter mark waiting for the whistle.

The game had been even until the third quarter, when the other team's hole set drove an elbow backward without looking. Yash had taken it across the temple going for the steal, and the sound of it carried underwater, a dull knock that Ryan felt in his own skull. Yash went under for a second, came up coughing, and swam to the lane rope on his own power, which everyone later agreed was the problem, because it made the hit look smaller than it was.

Coach pulled him out and sat him on the bench with a towel over his shoulders, and by the fourth quarter Yash was standing at the edge in his cap, jaw set, saying he was fine, saying it again, saying it a third time as though repetition were proof. Ryan was within earshot during a stoppage, close enough to hear Yash say, "Put me in. We're down two. I feel completely fine."

Ryan had read the concussion protocol sheet that Ms. Kowalski, the athletic director, had taped above the drinking fountain in September. He had read it twice, mostly out of boredom during a dryland session, and one line had stuck because it was so bluntly absolute: an athlete with a suspected concussion should not return to play on the same day, even if they feel fine. Not "should be evaluated," not "at the coach's discretion." Same day, no return, no exceptions for feeling fine. At the time it had seemed like paperwork. Now it seemed like the only sentence in the room worth saying.

He said it, quietly, because Yash was his friend and yelling would have made it a confrontation instead of a fact. "If there's a suspected concussion, the guidelines say you don't go back in the same day. Even if you feel fine." Yash turned on him with an expression Ryan would ruminate on for days afterward, a mixture of betrayal and contempt, as though Ryan had chosen the rules over him personally. "I don't have a concussion," Yash said. "I got hit." Ryan had no answer for the difference, if there was one, and the honest part of him knew that he didn't know whether Yash was concussed or just bruised and furious. Suspicion was not diagnosis. That was exactly why the rule was written the way it was, or maybe that was the reason Ryan invented afterward to make his own certainty feel earned. He couldn't tell.

The coach looked between them, then at the score, then made a small motion with his hand that kept Yash on the bench. They lost by one. In the locker room Yash dressed without speaking, and Noam, who had heard the whole exchange from the water, said only, "You did the right thing," which Ryan suspected was less a judgment than an act of solidarity, an artifice of friendship worn for the occasion, because Noam had been forty meters away and had no better idea than anyone whether Yash was hurt.

Two days later Yash sat out practice under the lights with a doctor's note, and he sat near Ryan on the deck, not apologizing but not leaving either, and the pool at night had a way of making everything around its edges look quiescent and slightly unreal, the water flat and glowing while the two of them sat in its light without talking about the game. "I wanted the final period," Yash said finally. "I've been playing this season like it's the only one that matters." Ryan understood that, and here was the part he could not resolve, even lying awake that week turning it over: wanting something badly is not a reason it should be granted, and yet it was not nothing either, it was the whole engine of the season, and the rule that had seemed so clean on the paper by the drinking fountain had a human cost that the paper did not mention. Both things were true. He held them at once the way you hold your breath underwater, waiting for the surface.

"Next season," Ryan said, "we're doing dryland first, and you're doing the swim test before anyone lets you near a ball." Yash splashed a handful of pool water at him, missing by half a meter, and the drops fell back onto the tile in a scatter of small bright rings.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At Lunar New Year, many Chinese families give money in red envelopes to children and unmarried younger relatives, because red is associated with good fortune and warding off evil.
story:
Michael had been standing in his grandmother's hallway for two minutes before he admitted to himself what he was doing, which was stalling. The house smelled of star anise and frying scallions, and through the kitchen doorway he could see aunts arguing pleasantly about the order of the dishes, and on the table by the door, next to the mandarin oranges, sat a small stack of red envelopes with gold characters pressed into the paper. Last year he had taken one without thinking, the way he had taken them since he was small. This year eighteen felt like a border he might have already crossed without noticing, and he could not decide whether it would be greedier to hold out his hand or ruder to refuse it.

He texted Jia from the safety of the hallway. "Serious question. Am I too old for the red envelopes?" Her reply arrived in pieces, the way her replies always did. "Define old." "Also define serious." Then, after a pause long enough that he pictured her setting down her chopsticks: "My cousin's twenty-four and still gets them. But she's my cousin, so who knows what that proves." Michael looked at the stack on the table. It proved something and nothing, which was Jia's speciality, and which was somehow less helpful than silence would have been.

His grandmother's neighbour, Mr. Shin, arrived at the door with a plate of sesame balls just as Michael was still hovering, and the two of them ended up wedged together in the entranceway while Michael's uncle shouted something welcoming from the kitchen. Mr. Shin was a saturnine man who tended to answer questions with questions, and when he noticed Michael glancing at the envelopes he raised one eyebrow in a way that invited explanation without promising any in return.

"It's the money in the red ones I'm wondering about," Michael said, keeping his voice low. "Whether I still count." Mr. Shin considered the table as though the envelopes themselves might settle it. "Children get them," he said finally. "Unmarried younger relatives too." Michael waited, and when nothing more came, he understood that he was being left to do the arithmetic himself. Eighteen. Not married, obviously, unless the state of Connecticut had made an error. Younger than everyone in this house except his cousin's toddler, who was currently attempting to eat a tangerine whole, peel and all.

He found his grandmother in the kitchen with her hands floury to the wrist, and he asked her, more directly than he had planned, why it was red specifically and not some other colour, gold maybe, which seemed the more obviously lucky choice to him. She wiped her hands on her apron and looked at him with an expression he couldn't read, somewhere between amusement and appraisal. "Red is good fortune," she said. "It wards off evil." Then she went back to the dough as if that were the entire history of the world and required no footnotes.

Michael carried a tray of cups into the dining room and thought about it while he set them down. What interested him was not the superstition itself but the logic underneath it, the way the custom drew a circle around certain people and said, you are still inside, you are still being looked after. He had spent a semester in biology listening to Mr. Shin's son, of all people, drone on about how you could find half a genotype in every cousin's face, and here was the same idea done with paper and money instead of chromosomes: the family locating you, claiming you, marking which side of grown you were standing on. He wasn't sure the two ways of thinking belonged in the same sentence, and he wasn't sure they didn't.

At the table, when the dishes had all landed and the aunts had stopped rearranging them, his grandmother picked up the stack of envelopes and moved around the circle in order of age, toddler first. Michael watched his own turn approach the way you watch a wave you can't tell whether to brace against or ride. When she reached him she paused, envelope held between two fingers, and studied him with the same unreadable expression from the kitchen. He understood suddenly that she was asking herself the same question he had been asking in the hallway, and that his answer and hers might not match, and that neither of them would ever say so out loud.

He held out both hands, and she laughed, a short surprised sound, and pressed the envelope into his palms and folded his fingers over it. Later, when the plates were being cleared, Jane texted to ask how the dinner had gone, and he started typing that he wasn't sure yet whether he was a kid or a grown-up, then deleted it, then typed instead, "Still employed as a grandson." He slid the envelope, unopened, into the inner pocket of his jacket, where he could feel its edge against his ribs every time he leaned forward to reach the tea.

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: Sea ice reflects most sunlight while open ocean absorbs most of it, so melting ice exposes darker water that warms and melts more ice: a reinforcing feedback loop.
story:
The hose at the community garden had been missing for eleven days, which the gardeners attributed to the mysterious economics of a place where nobody locked anything but everyone counted everything. Naomi had plot number fourteen, a rectangle of compromised soil where her tomatoes leaned sideways like commuters on a crowded bus. She had taken the plot in April with a plan involving canning, saving money, and proving something to her mother that she had not yet named. By August the plan had narrowed to keeping six plants alive under a watering restriction that allowed the hose on Tuesdays and Fridays before ten in the morning.

The heat that summer was not a topic so much as a condition, like gravity. Mr. Ionescu, who had plot number three and a system of stakes and twine that resembled rigging, said the city had raised the water rate because the reservoir was down, and the reservoir was down because it had not rained, and it had not rained because of things that happened elsewhere, in places none of them had voted for or against. He said this while tying up his peppers, not bitterly, the way a person reports the weather. Naomi noted it. In her science class the previous spring they had sketched something on the board about the Arctic: sea ice reflects most sunlight while the open ocean absorbs most of it, so when the ice melts it exposes darker water, and the darker water warms and melts more ice. Hiba had called it a reinforcing feedback loop, then immediately worried that she was showing off. It had seemed distant then, a diagram with arrows. It seemed less distant standing in a garden where the ground had cracked into a putative archipelago, islands of hard clay separating shallow green seas of mulch.

Emil, who had plot fifteen and therefore the bed next to hers, had a theory. His theory was that someone had cut the hose and absconded with it, probably to water a backyard grow-op, and that the neighborhood was in moral decline. He constructed this theory the way he constructed most things, loudly and with insufficient evidence, but he also showed up at six in the morning with two gallon jugs he had filled at his apartment and carried eight blocks, so Naomi had learned to separate the theory from the theorist.

The actual problem was smaller and worse than theft. On the second Tuesday of the restriction Naomi arrived early and found the spigot dripping, slow and constant, into a puddle that was itself evaporating in real time. She did the arithmetic standing there. A drip every two seconds, twelve hours a day when nobody was there, in a summer when the reservoir was down. It was not a crime. It was a washer, probably. But it was Hiba's diagram again, small enough to hold: something taken away, something darker and more absorbent exposed, the loss feeding the loss. She did not say this out loud, because saying it out loud would have made Emil start on the city council.

Instead she brought a five-gallon bucket on Wednesday and set it under the drip. Then she brought a second bucket. By Saturday there were four buckets in a row, and Mr. Ionescu had contributed an old curtain stretched over one of them to slow the evaporation, and Hiba, who biked past on her way to swim practice, stopped and asked what the buckets were for and stayed forty minutes past when she meant to leave.

They took the problem to the garden meeting, which was six people in folding chairs under the mulberry tree. Emil came prepared to accuse the neighborhood. He had a list. The list was, he conceded under questioning, mostly guesses. Naomi had brought the spigot handle she had unscrewed, with the worn washer inside it, and a jar of water showing what one night of dripping collected, about a gallon and a half. She also had the arithmetic about the hose schedule, which everyone had been treating as fairness and which she suggested treating as a system: two mornings of flooding and five days of dust made plants shallow-rooted and desperate, while water caught daily and spread thin kept them alive with less of it. She admitted she did not know whether the drip water was even allowed under the restriction, and that the buckets might breed mosquitoes, and that her tomatoes could still die. She said all of this because Hiba had once told her that a feedback loop was only honest if you said which parts you had not measured.

Emil stared at the washer for a while. Then he said, quietly for him, that the thief was a washer, and that he felt both better and stupider, and that he would bring his jugs on Thursdays now instead of Tuesdays if that helped the schedule. It was agreed. Someone volunteered to buy washers. Someone else, who had said nothing all meeting, mentioned that her grandfather caught rain off his garage roof and that nobody had ever restricted the sky.

They did not fix the climate, or the reservoir, or the rate increase, and by September three of Naomi's six tomatoes had died anyway. But the drip buckets stayed, and the mulberry tree meeting became monthly, and on the first cool morning of the fall Naomi found Hiba crouched at plot fourteen with a notebook, drawing arrows between the spigot, the buckets, the water bill, and the word reservoir, which she had misspelled and crossed out and misspelled again. "Loop," Hiba said, tapping it. "A small one. Ours."

"We haven't measured the mosquitoes," Naomi said.

"I'm counting them," Hiba said. "Eleven so far."

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: On a pyramid with five-year age groups, a bulge moves up one bar every five years, so today's large group of babies becomes a large group of schoolchildren soon after.
story:
The departures board flipped to DELAYED just as Lucas found seats near Gate 14, and Lionel dropped into the plastic chair beside him with the groan of someone who had already accepted ruin. Their connecting flight to the geography conference, where their presentation was due in fourteen hours, now showed a departure time four hours later than planned. Andreanne arrived carrying three coffees and a paper sleeve of napkins, handing one cup to a woman dozing two seats down who had been shivering in the airport air conditioning, and then she sat, spread the napkins on her knees, and opened the folder of census printouts.

"We still don't have an argument," Lucas said. "We have charts."

The assignment had seemed simple in September: analyse a population pyramid and predict whether the country needed more schools or nursing homes. Their town's pyramid looked like a top-heavy Christmas tree, wide at the fifty-to-seventy bars, narrow underneath, and Lucas had built the whole case around nursing homes. The numbers practically argued for themselves, he had told the class during their last rehearsal, gesturing at the grey bars with the confidence of a virtuoso who no longer needed to look at the score.

Andreanne smoothed a printout flat and tapped the bottom bars. "Except this."

At the base of the pyramid, in the zero-to-four group, there was a bulge. A wide, unmistakable band of babies, wider than the two bars above it, wider than anything else below the age of forty. Lucas had noticed it weeks ago and dismissed it, because the top of the pyramid was so much more dramatic, so obviously the story.

"That's four bars from the high school," Lionel said. He was tracing the bars upward with a pen cap, counting. "Zero to four, five to nine, ten to fourteen, fifteen to nineteen. Four bars."

"Which is what, twenty years?" Lucas said. "The nursing homes come first either way."

Andreanne pulled out a second sheet, the updated data their teacher, Mr. Rosen, had emailed them the night before, the reason they had been up until one in the morning printing. She laid it beside the first. "Look at the five-to-nine bar on the new one."

Lucas looked. On the old printout, the five-to-nine bar was thin. On the new one it was wide, wide as the baby bulge beneath it, and the baby bulge itself had been replaced at zero to four by a bar of ordinary size. He set down his coffee.

"It moved," he said.

"It moved up one bar," Andreanne said. "Five years, one bar."

The gate agent announced something about weather in Chicago, and the shivering woman thanked Andreanne for the coffee, and Lionel leaned over both sheets with his pen cap hovering between them like a needle between two magnets. Lucas felt the ground shift under his argument. If a bulge moves up one bar every five years, then the wide band of babies he had been ignoring was already a wide band of schoolchildren somewhere, and soon after, a wide band of teenagers lining up outside the high school doors. The two needs were not competing conclusions, one right and one wrong. They were both coming, in sequence, and the only real question was when.

"So the nursing homes for the current old people," Lionel said slowly, "and the schools for the babies, later."

"Soon after," Andreanne said, tapping the ascending bulge. "Not later-later."

A voice behind them said, "That's a better fight than the one you had in October," and they turned to find Mr. Rosen himself standing there with his boarding pass in his hand, two gates early for the same flight, holding a sandwich he clearly intended to eat standing up. Lucas braced for a lecture, for the prolix kind of correction Mr. Rosen was famous for, the fifteen-minute digressions that students timed like weather events. Instead Mr. Rosen just looked at the printouts and said nothing at all, which was somehow worse, because it meant they had to be the ones to say it.

"We had it backwards," Lucas said. "I mean, not exactly backwards. I built the whole thing on the top of the pyramid because it was bigger, and I treated the babies as, I don't know, a footnote."

"You treated them as the future," Andreanne said, not unkindly. "But the bars don't wait."

Mr. Rosen took a bite of his sandwich and said, "I'm just here for the sandwich," and moved off toward the windows, and Lucas understood that this was the whole lesson he was going to get, and that it was enough.

They rebuilt the presentation right there, napkins as scratch paper, Andreanne narrating while Lucas wrote and Lionel redraw the timeline on the back of a boarding-pass envelope. Lucas kept stopping himself from declaring the new argument airtight, because it wasn't; he could not say exactly when the bulge would reach the high school bar, only that it would arrive bar by bar, and that the town's planning committee, if it was honest, should be building both. He said as much out loud, and Lionel said, "That's a weaker thesis," and Andreanne said, "That's an honest one," and Lionel was quiet for a moment, turning his pen cap over, and then he said, "Fine. Honest it is. But we lead with the babies. Nobody expects the babies."

The shivering woman, wrapped now in a blanket the gate agent had brought her, watched them work with the mild interest of someone with four empty hours. When Lucas held up the two printouts side by side to check that the redrawn bars matched, she leaned over and said, "Which one's the future?" and Lucas pointed at the wide band climbing through the middle of the pyramid, one bar at a time, and said, "Both of them. Just not at the same time."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Before the Eid al-Fitr prayer, Muslims who can afford it give a set charity called zakat al-fitr for each family member, so that poor families can also celebrate Eid.
story:
Daniel's father counted the bills twice at the kitchen table the night before Eid, then counted them a third time, and Daniel, watching from the doorway with his coat already on, understood that something was wrong. "We're short," his father said. "Zakat al-fitr, before the prayer tomorrow, for everyone in the house." He laid a finger on each bill as if the money might confess. There was a rate per person, the same for every family that could afford it, and his father had calculated for six: himself, Daniel's mother, both grandmothers, Daniel, and his little sister. The seventh member of the household, Uncle Rahim, had arrived from the airport only that afternoon, suitcase still zipped in the hallway, and no one had remembered to add him until now.

The problem was simple and absolute. Their mosque distributed the collection in the morning, before the Eid al-Fitr prayer began, because the whole point was that poor families would have it in hand to celebrate the same day. After the prayer was too late. So at nine o'clock at night, in the first cold week of autumn, Daniel was crossing the little footbridge into Riverside Park with forty dollars of his father's money in an envelope inside his jacket, walking to the apartment of a man from the mosque who accepted early donations at his home near the far gate. His father had a bad knee and a phone call to make to his brother. Daniel had two working legs and, according to his father, a head that could be trusted with an errand of exactly this size and no larger.

The park at night was not the park of the afternoon. The basketball courts stood empty, their nets pale against the dark, and somewhere near the pond a radio played something tinny and far away. Daniel kept one hand in his jacket pocket, closed over the envelope, and thought about last year, when he had not been trusted with anything. Last year he had been the one who volunteered at the Eid fair in this same park, stacking juice boxes while his friends from school wandered past, and when Mederick had asked him why he bothered, Daniel had said something about it looking good on applications, which was partly true and mostly a lie, and Mederick had known it was mostly a lie, and had said nothing, which was worse than an argument.

A man stood under the lamp by the pond with a clipboard and a metal box, and when he saw Daniel he smiled with great warmth. "Collecting for the Eid," he called. "For the poor, brother, for tomorrow. Give here, save yourself the walk." Daniel slowed. The man's shoes were new and white, spotless in a park of mud and wet leaves, and his clipboard held no lists, only a few loose bills clipped under a corner. Daniel thought of a documentary he'd seen in history class about a medicine show, the way a charlatan could hold a crowd not by lying exactly but by never quite stating anything. The man had not said he was from the mosque. He had only let the park, the season and the phrase "for the poor" do the implying.

"I'm taking it to Mr. Hadid," Daniel said, naming the man from the mosque, and watched the stranger's smile reorganize itself. "Near the far gate." The stranger said that Mr. Hadid had moved, that the path was flooded, that he himself had been authorized, each sentence arriving a little too quickly, like a man exhume ing nothing so much as his own excuses, digging them up faster than Daniel could inspect them. Daniel said he'd check the flooded path himself. He walked on. Behind him the stranger called something generous-sounding about God rewarding him, and Daniel did not turn around.

Chaya found him at the far gate, which was the strange luck of a small city on a big night. She was coming from the opposite direction with her own family's envelope, because her mother had also realized late that a visiting cousin had to be counted, and the two of them stood on Mr. Hadid's stoop together while he unlocked the door, comparing errands like soldiers comparing marches. "Zakat al-fitr," Chaya said, holding up her envelope. "Every person in the house, before the prayer. Otherwise what's the point of it." Mr. Hadid, in slippers, took both envelopes and wrote two names in a real notebook with a real column of names above them, and Daniel saw his own money enter a ledger alongside a hundred others, and something in his chest settled.

Inside, over tea that neither of them had time for but that refusing would have been rude, Mr. Hadid mentioned that the boxes were already being sorted for delivery at dawn, so that families who had little would wake on Eid with something to spend on the day itself, a meal, sweets, new clothes for their children. The same celebration, the same morning, not a smaller version of it happening a week later. Daniel drank his tea and thought about the man by the pond, who had wanted the same bills for a different ledger, and about how close the two collections had sounded in the dark, one true and one hollow, distinguished by nothing you could prove to a stranger.

Walking home with Chaya along the lit path by the courts, they passed the pond again and the man was gone, leaving only the lamp and a rectangle of flattened grass where his box had stood. "You think anyone gave to him?" Chaya asked. Daniel said probably. She said that was awful, and he agreed, and then he disagreed with himself halfway through agreeing, because the people who had given had wanted to give, had reached into their pockets intending the poor, and maybe intention counted for something even when it landed in the wrong box, and maybe it counted for nothing at all, and he said so, both halves, and Chaya laughed and said he argued like her uncle.

The next morning the whole park was white paper and colored scarves, rows laid out across the soccer field, and Ms. Abdi from his chemistry class, there with her own family, waved at him across the crowd. His father's knee had survived the walk. His sister had new sandals she refused to take off even to sit down. The prayer had not yet begun; the boxes from the ledger, he knew, were already out in the city, in doorways and kitchens, doing whatever it was that money did when it arrived on time.

During the sermon Daniel kept his eyes open the way he always did, watching the slight movements of a thousand people trying to be still, and he found himself weighing last night against last year, the lie to Mederick against the envelope in his pocket, trying to decide whether he had become more honest or only more careful. He could not decide. The imam's voice went on, the crowd bent as one body, and his sister, three rows ahead, reached down without looking and slipped one sandal off, then, thinking better of it, put it back on.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: The stage manager records the blocking in the prompt book so that it can be repeated the same way at every performance.
story:
My grandmother's parlour has the best light in the county, which is why I told everyone the rehearsals had to happen there, and not, as Adrien kept insisting, because I wanted an excuse to be looked after for a week. Her house sits at the end of Fir Street with a wide bay window and a floor that slopes just enough that a chair left alone will drift, very slowly, toward the kitchen. I had claimed the parlour for the one-act I was directing, my first, and I had exactly six days before Friday's performance in the school hall.

"You're the director," Laurence said on Monday, dropping his bag by the door. "So direct us. Where do I go?"

That was the problem. I had read that directing meant having a vision, and I had one, or thought I did, something about two brothers in a room that keeps getting smaller. But a vision, it turned out, did not tell Laurence where to put his feet. Adrien stood by the mantel waiting, and my grandmother put down tea nobody had asked for, and I said the first thing that came into my head: "Maybe you cross to the window when you say the line about the river."

He crossed. It looked, I will admit, terrible, like a man walking toward a bus. But I wrote it down anyway, in a school notebook, because writing things down felt like directing. Cross window on river line. Then I changed it Tuesday and again Wednesday, and each time I told myself the new version had been the plan all along, which was easier than admitting I was guessing.

Mr. Ross, the neighbour from two doors down, came Thursday with a folding ruler he thought my grandmother might want. He had run theatre in another life, he said, before teaching, before his sabbatical year turned permanent. He watched ten minutes of our rehearsal from the doorway with his coat still on. I wanted to tell him we were fine, that the drifting chairs were intentional, that the stopping and restarting was a technique, but he'd been around long enough to know a lie told politely.

"Who keeps your prompt book?" he asked.

"My what?"

He didn't lecture, to his credit. He just nodded at my notebook, the fat school one with the coffee ring, and said, "The stage manager records the blocking in the prompt book so it can be repeated the same way at every performance." Then he asked about the weather and left, taking his ruler, and Adrien and I stood there in the sloping parlour understanding that we had been treating the whole week as a draft.

We rebuilt that afternoon. Adrien, who had the tidiest handwriting, sat with the notebook and a pencil and became, by common agreement, our stage manager. Every cross, every turn, every drift of a chair went in. Laurence downstage left at the letter. Adrien crosses to him, two steps, on "you never wrote back." I stopped inventing and started deciding, which felt less glamorous and more like carpentry. Was it my vision still, if half of it was Adrien's neat columns? I didn't ask that out loud. I asked whether the window cross should be on the river line or after it, and we tried both, and after won, and after went in the book.

Friday came faster than Fridays are supposed to. Backstage at the hall, Laurence gripped my sleeve ten minutes before curtain and said, "Do I cross to him before she comes in, or after?"

"After," I said, with total authority, and I would swear to this day it was after, though Adrien's book, when I checked, said before, in his small careful hand, dated Thursday, initialled. Which of us had said what on Thursday I could no longer reconstruct. My memory of the week had gone soft and flattering, every choice mine, every choice good.

They argued in the wings, actually argued, Laurence hot and certain, Adrien cold and flipping pages. "The stage manager records the blocking in the prompt book," Adrien said, "so it can be repeated the same way at every performance. That's the whole point. It's before." And Laurence looked at me to overrule it, and I opened my mouth, and what came out was, "Show him the page." He looked at the page. He crossed before she came in, and the moment landed better than anything we'd done in my grandmother's parlour, the timing tighter, the room smaller the way I'd wanted, though whether that was the blocking or the fear I couldn't say.

Afterwards my grandmother found me near the props table. She pressed a wrapped biscuit into my hand, which did something to assuage the hollow, rattling feeling in my chest, though not everything. She said I looked like my grandfather after his first sermon, which I took as praise until I remembered he'd been a vacuum salesman.

On the walk back to Fir Street, past Mr. Ross's dark windows, I kept turning it over. The notebook was in Adrien's bag, and I would have to ask him for it, or copy it, or let it go. Monday I would start the next one-act. I thought maybe I'd direct it looser, trust the actors more, and I thought, in almost the same breath, that I'd write everything down twice. The streetlight at the corner buzzed and steadied. Adrien stopped at his gate and held up the bag.

"You want the book?" he said.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Socialist politician Jean Jaurès wrote a socialist history of the French Revolution in the early 1900s that shaped the class-conflict interpretation dominant for much of the twentieth century.
story:
The memorial sat at the edge of the park where the town stopped pretending to be anything but fields, a granite obelisk with forty-one names carved into its base. Jordan had walked past it on the way to school for eleven years without once reading them, and now he read them twice, because Mr. Hughes had assigned the historiography essay and told them, almost as an afterthought, that history was not just what happened but what people decided it meant afterward. The topic sat on Jordan's screen at home like a locked door: how views of the French Revolution had changed since 1800. Two weeks of reading and all he had was a pile of quotations that disagreed with each other and no idea how to make them into anything.

Veronica was already at the memorial when he arrived, cross-legged on the bottom step with her laptop balanced on her knee, because she claimed she worked better in cold air. She had chosen the same topic. Mitchell had chosen the Cold War and had finished a draft in three days, which Jordan found quietly unbearable.

"There's a French name down here," Veronica said, tilting her head at the low panel of the base. "Jaures or something. Jean Jaurès. Was our town full of French soldiers?"

Jordan crouched beside her. The stone said the man had died in 1914, and it said nothing else, which struck him as its own kind of sentence, a full stop with no clause before it. "Maybe he lived here. Maybe he taught at the old school."

"Look him up, then. You're the one who needs distraction from your blank document."

He typed the name into his phone, half expecting a farmer. The first line said he was a socialist politician, assassinated in 1914. The second line said he had written a socialist history of the French Revolution in the early 1900s. Jordan read it three times, then held the phone out to Veronica without a word, which was unlike him, and she took it, which was unlike her, and for a moment they were two people staring at a small glowing rectangle in front of forty-one carved names.

"So he wasn't local at all," she said. "Someone put him on our memorial anyway."

"Maybe the person who chose the names liked his politics. Or maybe they just had a list of the Great War's dead famous men and didn't check where they lived."

"It's a bit like a lie, though. A small one."

Jordan sat down on the step. He was thinking about the essay again, but differently now, the way a puzzle looks different once one piece is turned the right way up. He scrolled further and found a historian describing how Jaurès's account, with its insistence on class conflict as the engine of the Revolution, had dominated the interpretation for much of the twentieth century. Before that, the books Jordan had skimmed, the ones from 1800 onward, had mostly been about great men and ideas, about whether the whole thing was a triumph or a catastrophe. Somewhere in between, the question had quietly become about classes instead.

"Here's the thing," he said. "The facts of the Revolution didn't change. The guillotine didn't move. But what people thought it meant changed completely, and not because of new evidence, at least not mostly. It changed because of who was asking."

Veronica looked up. "You sound like Hughes."

"Hughes would say it better. He'd use some word for understatement, like litotes, and I'd want to throw something." She laughed at that, and he noticed she'd closed her own laptop, which she never did. "But look at this guy. A politician who writes history. He gets shot, and his book outlives him and ends up shaping a hundred years of argument. Then a guy like me finds him on a war memorial in a town he never visited, because somebody in 1919 or whenever had an opinion."

"Or a grudge," Veronica said. "Or a hero. You can't know which."

Jordan thought about the first draft he had tried to write, the one where he planned to pick a side, declare the Revolution's legacy good or bad, and defend it with the confidence he'd been rewarded for in every essay since he was twelve. It occurred to him now that the assignment was not asking for a verdict at all. It was asking him to stand where Jaurès had stood, and where the memorial's unknown chooser had stood, and describe the view from each place without pretending the view was the landscape. The class-conflict story felt true to him, he admitted, more true than tales of heroes and ideas, but he could not fully separate that feeling from the fact that he had been born into a century that Jaurès's followers had largely written. Whether the interpretation had conquered because it was right or because its moment had come, he genuinely did not know, and he suspected the distinction was the whole essay.

"I'm going to write about the historians as characters," he said. "Not the revolutionaries. The historians."

"That's not what the assignment says."

"It's what the assignment means. I think. I hope." He paused. "There's this other thing. Earlier drafts kept making the older historians sound stupid, like they were blind because they didn't see class. My dad does that, actually. Anyone who disagrees with him is obviously pathologized, something wrong with them, not just positioned differently. I don't want to write like my dad."

Veronica grinned. "That is the most honest thing you've ever said about your father."

"The evidence for them being wrong is mostly that later people disagreed with them. That's not nothing, but it's thinner than I first thought. Some of what looked like bias is just what questions their world made it possible to ask. The rest of it, the ancillary stuff, the footnotes they chose, who they dedicated things to, I barely know what to do with any of that yet."

They sat while the light went flat and grey behind the obelisk. Mitchell cycled past on the far path, saw them, braked in a long skid, and called out that his essay was done and asked whether theirs was. Veronica said, "Not a chance," and Mitchell laughed and rode on, and Jordan pulled out his notebook and wrote Jaurès's name at the top of a blank page, followed by a question he did not yet have an answer for. Then he stood and traced the carved letters once with his finger, the way he had seen old men do at memorials in films, and had never understood until now.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: Progressive overload means gradually increasing training demands, such as weight, distance or intensity, so the body keeps having a reason to adapt.
story:
Madeline had been running the same loop in Hartwell Park since March, three miles every Saturday, and by June she could run it no faster than she had in April. She had the times written in the back of her chemistry notebook to prove it: 27:40, 27:12, 27:38, 27:15. She was lying on the grass near the water fountain with her shoes off when Cassie sat down beside her and stole a sip of her water.

"You look like someone doing math in her head about something that isn't math," Cassie said.

"I run the same thing every week and nothing changes. Shouldn't it change? I'm not tired afterward anymore. That has to count for something."

Cassie pulled up short, which for Cassie meant a full ten seconds of silence. "My cousin does rowing. She says when a workout gets easy it's not an achievement, it's a message. The body has no reason to change if you don't ask it for more." She dug in her bag for the protein bar she always kept for emergencies and split it. "She calls it progressive overload. Increasing the demands a bit at a time, weight or distance or intensity, so the body keeps having to adapt."

Madeline sat up so fast she got dizzy. "Wait. Say the last part again." She wrote it in the notebook, under the times, in handwriting that got worse the more excited she got. "So I've been maintaining. For three months I've been paying a membership fee to stay exactly the same."

"Cheerful," Cassie said. "Want the other half of the bar? It tastes like drywall but it's yours."

That night Madeline drew up a plan, and the plan immediately began to adjudicate between two voices in her head. One voice sounded like her own and wanted to add a mile to every run, starting tomorrow, because she had wasted three months and needed to catch up. The other voice sounded, embarrassingly, like her gym teacher from ninth grade, the one who had made them do warm-ups and then jog laps while he read the newspaper, and it kept saying something about rest days that Madeline had never bothered to write down. The result was an inchoate document, half schedule and half argument with herself, with arrows crossing things out. She carried it to the park the next morning, where Quinten was already on the bench by the basketball courts, eating a bagel like it owed him money.

"Is that a battle plan or a grocery list?" he said.

"It's a training program. Four runs a week. One long, one with hills, one easy, and one where I go faster than comfortable for short bits. Monday off, Thursday off, warm-up before every one." She tapped the page. "The rest days are the part I don't believe in. Sitting still feels like the opposite of progress."

Quinten considered this with the seriousness he usually reserved for fantasy football. "My dad tore something in his shoulder doing the same twelve pushups every night for a year. Then he did fifty on a Saturday because he was angry about a parking ticket, and now he can't lift the good chair." He brushed crumbs off his shorts. "Maybe the in-between is where the magic is. Or the injury. One of the two."

The first new Saturday, Madeline ran three and a half miles and finished with her hands on her knees, breathing like a landed fish, delighted. The second week her shins ached and she cut the fast run short, walking the last half mile past the paddleboats while she recalculated on her phone, moving the long run from Sunday to Tuesday, because the schedule had to bend or she would break. By the fourth week she noticed something she hadn't expected: she looked forward to Mondays. To the day with nothing in the box. Rest, it turned out, was not the absence of the plan but a column in it, and that idea rearranged more than her running. She started leaving Thursday nights empty too, no homework pushed to midnight, and her mother noticed before she did, saying only, "You're quieter lately," in a tone that Madeline could not fully read.

In late July she ran the loop in 25:05, and then, the following week, 25:05 again, and she stood at the water fountain trying to decide whether that was failure or just the message arriving a second time, telling her the next small demand was waiting. It was a kind of synchronicity, she supposed, that Cassie happened to walk up at that exact moment, holding two ice creams she'd clearly bought to celebrate a time she hadn't yet heard.

"So?" Cassie said, holding one out. "Was it worth rebuilding everything?"

Madeline took it, and looked down at the melted drip winding toward her knuckle, and shrugged. "Ask me in October." Then she started walking, because the ice cream was losing the race against the sun.

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: Canada's 2019 food guide suggests filling half the plate with vegetables and fruits, a quarter with protein foods and a quarter with whole grain foods.
story:
Brooklyn found the list crumpled at the bottom of her tote, half of it printed in the basement of the school library two days earlier, half of it rewritten on the bus in her own cramped hand. At the top, underlined twice, was the note she had copied from the Health Canada page: half the plate vegetables and fruits, a quarter protein foods, a quarter whole grain foods. Ms. Shevchenko had not assigned it. She had only said, on the last day of the food and nutrition unit, that if any of them planned to live on residence food for four years, that was their business, but that the ones who wanted to cook should learn before September. Brooklyn had wanted to cook, suddenly and specifically, the way you want something only after you learn it exists.

The market opened at eight and she arrived at 8:40 with forty dollars in cash and a folding cart that had belonged to her grandmother. Imane came with her, partly for company and partly because Imane's mother had sent her for eggs. Imane was loquacious before ten in the morning in a way Brooklyn had stopped fighting years ago, and she narrated the stalls as they passed: the honey man who never made change quickly, the bread table where you had to arrive early or settle for scones, the lettuce that looked better than the lettuce at the grocery store and cost the same.

"Your list is organized weird," Imane said, reading over her shoulder while Brooklyn counted out toonies for a bundle of kale. "It's all vegetables first."

"Half the plate," Brooklyn said. "That's the rule I'm using. Vegetables and fruits are half, protein's a quarter, whole grains the other quarter. So the list is half produce by, like, volume." She said it and heard how it sounded, a rule recited rather than understood, and she was aware of Imane watching her fold the kale into the cart with more care than kale required.

At home there would be five evenings to feed herself, because her mother had taken the contract in Sudbury and left the kitchen to her with a shrug that was meant as confidence but landed somewhere else. Brooklyn had signed nothing, but she had written the plan on the whiteboard like an affidavit: Monday lentils and rice, Tuesday roast vegetables with eggs, Wednesday the leftover lentils reheated, Thursday soup, Friday whatever remained. The plan's virtue was that it could survive one bad night. Its flaw was that she had never made any of it before.

The trouble came at the root vegetable stall. She needed carrots and potatoes for the roasting tray, but the quantities on her list had been guesswork, and the smallest bag of potatoes held more than the plan required. While she stood doing arithmetic against the whiteboard in her head, Audrey-Ann appeared beside her, holding a single enormous beet as if she had won it.

"You're doing the plate thing," Audrey-Ann said. "Imane told me. She said you bought a shocking amount of kale."

"It wasn't shocking."

"It was five bunches."

"It was three." Brooklyn paid for the potatoes, and then, because the bag was heavier than she'd expected, she redistributed it between the cart and her arms. "The half is the hard part. At home we always did, like, a slab of meat and then sides. My mom's version of a vegetable is frozen peas poured into a bowl. If I follow the plate, the meat shrinks and everything else has to double, and I don't actually know what a week of that looks like in a shopping cart."

Audrey-Ann turned the beet over in her hands. "So you're finding out."

"I'm finding out the expensive way, possibly."

The vendor, wrapping the beet in newspaper, mentioned without being asked that a half bushel of canning tomatoes was going cheap at the end of the row, and Brooklyn walked down there and stood in front of them for a long minute. Fifty pounds of tomatoes was a commitment to a self she had not yet met, someone who canned things, someone whose Sundays had a shape. She bought a smaller basket instead, and eggs, and a rye loaf from the bread table, and she did not buy the honey because forty dollars turned out to be a number that ran out.

Sunday afternoon, in her mother's kitchen, she roasted the carrots and half the potatoes with oil and the rosemary she'd had to exhume from the back of the spice cupboard, dried to something like dust but still fragrant when she crushed it. She cooked the lentils in a pot too large for them and laid out five containers on the counter, dividing by eye, checking each one against the proportions she'd written at the top of the list. The lentils looked small in their quarter of the container. The kale, blanched and squeezed, took up more room than anything else, which was either the plan working or a mistake she wouldn't recognize until Thursday.

Imane texted a photo of her own eggs with a caption that read "protein quarter." Brooklyn sent back the open containers, then turned off her phone and sat on the kitchen floor with the last warm potato, eating it with her fingers straight from the tray while the afternoon light moved across the counter and the five containers waited, lined up and imperfect, for the week.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: Albert Mehrabian's often-quoted '7 percent words, 38 percent tone, 55 percent face' rule came from experiments on conveying feelings, and he said it does not apply to all communication.
story:
The number 41 bus smelled of wet raincoats and orange peel, and Isaac boarded it holding a printed page of interview questions like it was a rare manuscript. Andy slid over to make room, saw the page, and grinned so widely that Isaac sat down anyway, braced.

"You're doing the Fish Shack thing," Andy said. "Saturday. Ten o'clock. You told Leonie in the cafeteria and she told me, which by the way is how information works in this town."

"I told her not to tell you."

"Then you don't understand syllogisms," Andy said, tapping his temple. "Leonie tells me everything, therefore you told me. Also I have something that will change your life." He produced his phone, already loaded, because Andy's phone was always already loaded. "Ninety-three percent of communication is not words. Seven percent words, thirty-eight percent tone, fifty-five percent your face. It's science. A guy named Mehrabian."

Isaac took the phone. There it was, in a listicle with clip art of brains: a statistic that seemed, for one seismic moment, to let him off the hook entirely. He had spent three evenings trying to memorize why he wanted to work at a fish counter, and now the internet was telling him the words barely counted at all. "So I just have to look trustworthy," he said slowly. "And sound calm. And say literally anything."

"You could recite the periodic table," Andy said. "Confidently. With eye contact."

Across the aisle, Leonie lowered her camera, which she had been aiming at the fogged window. "I need you both to keep talking," she said. "I'm making a documentary for media class about the last week of school, and you two are my best footage. Andy fell asleep on this bus on Tuesday and I got fourteen seconds of him snoring with his mouth open. That's my most-watched clip."

"That's a violation," Andy said, without any real heat, because being filmed was the price of sitting near Leonie and he had accepted the terms long ago.

Isaac tried an experiment right there. He looked Andy dead in the eye, kept his voice level and warm, and said, "I believe my greatest weakness is that I care too much about fish."
