Andy nodded along, visibly soothed, for about four seconds, and then burst out laughing so hard the man in front of them turned around. "Okay," Andy wheezed, "okay, the face worked, the voice worked, and then the words arrived and destroyed everything. The words are landmines, Isaac."

They ran it again on the ride past the hardware store, Leonie filming with the microphone held out between the seats like an offering. Isaac answered why he wanted the job, what his availability was, how he'd handle an angry customer, and each time Andy excoriated the performance with the joy of a professional critic. "You looked at the ceiling during availability. The ceiling, Isaac. The ceiling can't hire you." Isaac was laughing too, but underneath the laughing something was bothering him, an itch of arithmetic. If only seven percent was words, why did one bad sentence blow the whole thing up? He kept scrolling on Andy's phone, past the clip art, and found a longer page, one with actual paragraphs, written by people who apparently read books.

"Wait," he said. The bus swayed around the long corner by the park. "It says here the numbers came from experiments about conveying feelings. Like whether a listener believes someone who says they like something while sounding annoyed. That's what the seven, thirty-eight, fifty-five was about. Feelings." He looked up. "It wasn't about interviews at all. Mehrabian himself said it doesn't apply to all communication."

Andy peered at the screen with the expression of a man watching a magic trick get explained. "So the internet took a thing about feelings and used it on everything?"

"Basically."

"So my whole strategy of smiling through the periodic table..."

"Was a house built on sand," Isaac said, and felt oddly pleased with himself, and then, because honesty was creeping up on him the way it did, less pleased. "Except," he went on, "the numbers aren't nothing, right? The face and the voice did work. For four whole seconds. You almost believed I cared too much about fish. Maybe the true thing is stupider than either version. The words matter, and the face and voice also matter, and Mehrabian's rule is only true when you're talking about how you feel."

Leonie lowered the camera. "Say the last part again," she said. "Facing me this time. That's going in the documentary, I've decided it's the thesis."

He said it again, facing her, and this time he noticed he was looking at her the whole way through, and his voice had settled into something that wasn't a performance, and the sentence came out clean. "Huh," he said. Andy clapped once, slowly, like a man at a golf tournament.

The bus hissed to a stop at the corner where the Fish Shack's neon sign was visible two blocks down, blinking its half-dead OPEN. Isaac folded the question sheet, not because he'd decided it didn't matter but because he'd decided it did, mostly, probably, in a way he'd have to test on Saturday at ten. "Practice tonight?" Andy asked, standing to pull the cord.

"One hour," Isaac said. "And if I say the periodic table, you have to tell me."

"Fish," Andy said solemnly, stepping down onto the curb. "If you say the periodic table, I will recite fish at you."

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: Circumlocution, describing a word you cannot remember instead of stopping, is a recognized communication strategy that keeps a second-language speaker talking.
story:
The kitchen smelled of cardamom and burnt sugar, and Arianna spread her flashcards across the table where her grandfather's newspapers usually sat. In three days she would stand in front of a classroom and argue, entirely in French, for five minutes, on whether the city should lower the voting age to sixteen. She could conjugate verbs in her sleep. What she could not do was survive the moment when a word vanished on her, which had happened twice during rehearsal and both times she had stopped, gone silent, and watched her teacher, Mr. Chan, make a small note on his clipboard.

Her grandmother moved between the stove and the counter, ignoring the cards, until Arianna said the French word for tax wrong three times in a row and put her head down on the table. Then the old woman laughed, a short sound like a door unlatching, and sat across from her.

"You stop," her grandmother said. "Why do you stop?"

"Because I don't know the word."

"So say the word you know. My mother crossed a border with one sentence and a basket of plums. When she wanted to say money, she said the paper the government asks for. When she wanted the doctor, she said the man who fixes the body." She tapped the table twice. "My sister, the teacher, she called it circumlocution. Talking around a hole instead of falling in it."

Arianna lifted her head. She had never heard the word before, but she recognized the shape of the thing immediately, the way you recognize a face you had only seen in bad photographs. That evening she tried it on Aiden over video call, having him throw English prompts at her while she answered in French. "The money the government takes from working people," she said, when tax deserted her, and kept going, and the sentence held. Aiden grinned and told her she sounded like a politician, which she chose to take as a compliment.

The cost showed itself the next morning. She had spent so long talking around words that she had stopped drilling the words themselves, and when Amber quizzed her on the list, Arianna missed nine. Amber, who had a knack for the merciless, excoriated her for it, in the affectionate way friends have of being terrible. "You're building a whole beautiful detour," Amber said, "and forgetting there's supposed to be a road." They fought about it for ten minutes, and then Arianna went back to the flashcards with her ears burning, because Amber was right and being right made her no less annoying.

At her grandmother's house that afternoon, Arianna rehearsed the full five minutes standing in the hallway where her grandfather's coat still hung, though he had been gone since spring. She argued that sixteen-year-olds paid taxes on their paycheques and rode buses the city ran and should therefore have a say. Halfway through, the word for election left her entirely. She felt the silence opening under her tongue, and instead of stopping she said the day when everyone marks a paper to choose the leaders, and her voice did not break, and the sentence carried her across the gap like a plank across a ditch.

Afterward her grandmother said nothing for a while. Then she said, "Your grandfather had an aphorism for everything. Slow is smooth, smooth is fast. He drove me crazy with them." She smoothed the sleeve of the coat with one hand. "But he also said a borrowed word never fits as well as your own, and on that one he was wrong. Half of what he ever said to me in this country was borrowed. It still fit." It was the first time Arianna understood that her grandmother had done all this decades ago, in the other direction, English instead of French, and had never once mentioned it, not in all the years of Sunday dinners.

The morning of the debate, Mr. Chan reminded them that a gratuitous pause would cost points, and Arianna almost laughed out loud, because she had a plan for pauses now, and it was better than the points. Standing up, she began in French, and for two and a half minutes every word arrived on time, obedient, polished. Then, in front of everyone, the word for tax walked out of her head with no notice at all.

She heard Amber exhale in the second row. She heard her own heart. "The money," Arianna said, in French, slowly enough that it sounded deliberate, "that the government takes from working people, from girls like me with paycheques, from my grandmother's pension." A boy in the back started writing something down. Mr. Chan did not reach for his clipboard. She kept going, past the four-minute mark, past her own certainty about whether she was winning, and finished with both sides of the argument still arguing inside her, out loud, at the same time.

"How long have you been able to do that?" Amber asked her afterward in the hall.

"Since Tuesday," Arianna said. "Ask me again in five years."

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: Signalling before a merge or lane change warns other drivers of the move; signalling too late, or not at all, gives them no time to adjust.
story:
The parking lot behind Fioretti's Grocery was empty on Sunday mornings, which was exactly why Camille's father chose it for parallel parking practice. He set two shopping carts in the aisles of the lot to stand in for the car ahead and the car behind, and Camille backed between them, over and over, until her neck ached from looking over her shoulder. The town was a littoral one, all salt and gulls and streets that ended in water, and the store sat on the last dry block before the harbour road, so every failed attempt had a backdrop of masts and low tide. She had failed the road test once already. The examiner's pencil had crossed out the merge on the highway ramp, and her father's face afterwards had been a study in stoicism, which was somehow worse than anger.

"You're looking at the carts," her father said through the window on the fifth attempt. "Look where you want the car to go."

"I want the car to go between the carts."

"Then look at the space, not the carts."

She thought about that while she reversed, easing the wheel, straightening, and when she opened her door to check, both carts stood untouched, with a sidewalk's worth of room behind her. She sat there for a moment, engine ticking, wondering why nobody had ever told her that your eyes led your hands, and whether that was true of other things too, or only steering.

On Monday she told Aryanna and Emma-Rose about it in the produce section, where they all worked after school, weighing grapes and restacking onions that customers forever rummaged through. "The whole test is next Saturday," Camille said, loading limes into the pyramid. "Parking's fine now. It's the merge I can't do."

"Then let's drive the ramp," Aryanna said, as though it were obvious. "After close. Mr. Popescu can follow in his car."

Mr. Popescu ran the store, a compact man who had learned to drive in a country with different rules entirely and never let anyone forget it. He agreed, on the condition that they sweep first, and so at nine that night three cars climbed the on-ramp by the harbour, Camille's father silent in the passenger seat, the headlights of Mr. Popescu's little hatchback glowing behind them like patience itself.

She signalled as she turned the wheel onto the ramp itself, a quick flick, almost decorative, and in the mirror Mr. Popescu's headlights blinked twice, hard. When they pulled into the lot afterwards he walked up to her window, and she rolled it down to the smell of night and cooling asphalt. "You signal before you move," he said. "Not while you're already moving. The signal is a warning before, so the other driver has time to do something about it. Too late, and what can they do? Nothing. They had no time."

I turned the wheel and the signal and the merge all into one motion, Camille thought, sitting very still while Mr. Popescu's headlights raked the lot. Like the carts. I was looking at the wrong thing, only this time the wrong thing was the moment itself. A signal flicked on in the middle of a merge wasn't a signal at all; it was an announcement of something already finished, a courtesy after the fact, and the driver behind her had been given nothing to work with. She wondered how far ahead a warning needed to travel before it counted as one, and whether you could ever really know, since every driver behind you was a stranger moving at their own speed with their own evening in their head.

They ran the ramp again, three times, four. On the fifth pass she flicked the lever a full breath before she drifted toward the gap, and in the mirror the car behind, not Mr. Popescu's this time but a stranger's pickup, eased off almost gently, opening space like a door held open. Her father said nothing. She merged into the lit ribbon of the highway, the harbour lying black to her left, and heard her own breathing.

On Saturday she sat in the examiner's car outside the test centre, hands on the wheel at ten and two, and when the ramp came she signalled early, held it, watched the mirror, moved. The examiner's pencil stayed still. In the parking lot afterwards, Aryanna and Emma-Rose were waiting on the curb with a bag of grapes from the store, and Camille held up the paper with its single red stamp while the gulls wheeled over the harbour behind them.

"So can you drive us somewhere now?" Emma-Rose asked.

"Get in," Camille said, and reached over and unlocked the door.

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: According to Acts 15 in the New Testament, a meeting of the early church in Jerusalem decided that non-Jewish converts to Christianity did not need to be circumcised.
story:
The debate club met on Wednesday evenings in the basement of St. Brigid's, in a room that smelled of instant coffee and hymnal dust, and Jason had come because his mother had signed the permission slip before he could argue. Genesis was already there, flipping through a binder, and Lennox was leaning against the radiator, testing how far back it would tip before it banged against the wall.

Mr. Wright, who taught the club and repaired the church boiler on weekends, wrote a question on the whiteboard in dry-erase marker that was running dry: Do ancient religious rules still apply in modern life? "You can't just tell me your opinion," he said. "You have to argue from the text itself. Whatever book you were assigned, it has to do the talking."

Jason had been assigned the New Testament, and specifically the Book of Acts, which he had not read beyond the Christmas parts. He'd assumed the assignment would be easy in the way a forfeit is easy: the old rules were old, the modern world was modern, and the two had nothing to say to each other. Genesis was arguing the other side, that the rules were permanent, and she had already found her verse and highlighted it in three colors.

They had two weeks. That first Wednesday, Genesis cross-examined him in front of everyone, and he had nothing. "So you think a rule written two thousand years ago just stops counting?" she said. "Who decides when? You?" Jason said something about progress, and Lennox, from the radiator, said, "That's not an argument, that's a vibe," and Mr. Wright did not disagree, which was worse.

So Jason took the Bible home. He read it at the kitchen table while his father watched golf with the sound off, and at first he skimmed, looking for ammunition, anything that sounded like rules being cancelled. He found laws, lots of them, and then he found something he had not expected: an argument. In chapter fifteen of Acts, there was a meeting in Jerusalem where the early church had to decide what to do with non-Jewish converts, whether the old rule about circumcision applied to them. Some said it did. Some said it didn't. And the meeting decided it didn't.

He read the chapter twice, then a third time, holding his finger under the line where the decision landed. Nobody in the story said the rule had never mattered. They said something narrower, and it took him a while to see the shape of it: the text itself showed believers arguing over which old rules still applied, and deciding, out loud, in a room. The rule about circumcision, the one their own scriptures required, was set aside for the new converts by the people closest to its origin. Not discarded. Distinguished.

The following Wednesday he brought the book with a pad of sticky notes bristling from it, and Genesis saw them and rolled her eyes. "You found something," she said. It wasn't a question. Mr. Wright set up two chairs at the front, and Lennox volunteered to keep time, then used the stopwatch on his phone to time Mr. Wright pouring coffee, so he was replaced.

"I used to think the choice was keep the rules or throw them out," Jason said. "But the people in Acts didn't do either. There was a real dispute, and they held a meeting in Jerusalem, and the decision was that Gentile converts, non-Jewish converts, didn't need to be circumcised. That's in the book. So the book shows the first generation already debating this exact question, which rules carried over and which didn't. If they could ask it, I can ask it."

Genesis didn't answer right away. She turned a page in her binder, slowly, buying herself the seconds. "Okay," she said. "But they had apostles in the room. Who was basically an eyewitness. We have us. That's like letting the recalcitrant kid in the back row rewrite the honor code because he read the handbook." A couple of people laughed. Jason wrote down recalcitrant because he didn't want to ask what it meant in front of everyone.

"That's actually my point," he said. "I'm not saying anyone can expropriate the text for whatever they want. You can't just take it. But I'm also not saying the rules are a wall nobody touched. It's more like an apportionment. The Acts meeting divided things up, what applied to whom, and they used the text to do it, they didn't ignore it. So the answer isn't yes or no. It's: by what standard do you sort them, and who has the standing to sort?"

Mr. Wright leaned against the desk with his cup. "And what's your standard?" he asked. Jason looked at his notes and found he had written the question at the top of the page and nothing under it. "I don't have one yet," he said. "I know the sorting happened. I don't know yet how I'd do it myself. If I say love your neighbor overrides everything, I've just picked a rule I like and called it the standard. Somebody else picks a different one. That's the part I haven't solved."

Genesis capped her highlighter. "So you're going to stand up on Friday and tell the judges your conclusion is that you don't have a conclusion." "No," Jason said. "My conclusion is that the text gives us a method, an argument in a room, and the method is the answer even when the outcome isn't obvious. The outcome depends on the question." Lennox, off duty now, said, "That's the most lawyer thing I've ever heard." Jason flipped back to chapter fifteen and slid the Bible across the table to Genesis, his finger holding the place. "Read the decision part," he said. "Then tell me if I'm wrong."

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: Exegesis means drawing a text's meaning out of its words and context, while eisegesis means reading one's own ideas into it, a distinction used to judge interpretations of scripture.
story:
The argument started over the folding table, which John's uncle had set up in the backyard between the potato salad and the pitcher of lemonade. Guneet had come with John to the family gathering because his own house was empty that weekend, and Gillian had tagged along because she wanted to watch John lose. That was how she put it. She had a debate tournament flyer folded into her back pocket, and the resolution printed on it was whether an ancient religious rule still binds people who no longer live in the world that made it.

"You can't just say a rule is old," Gillian said, spearing a forkful of salad. "Old isn't an argument. You have to go to the text itself and pull the meaning out of it. That's the whole assignment."

Guneet leaned forward. "And you can't smuggle your own opinions in dressed up as the text's opinions. Mr. Augustin called that the worst sin in interpretation. Exegesis means drawing a text's meaning out of its words and context, and eisegesis means reading your own ideas into it. He made us repeat it."

John had been quiet through the potato salad, and not only because his mouth was full. The rule in question came from a passage his grandmother knew by heart, one about rest and work, and he had grown up watching the family keep it loosely, the way people keep an old coat that no longer fits but still hangs by the door. His uncle ran his shop seven days a week now. His grandmother said nothing about it, which was itself a position, though nobody could quote it.

"So give me the verse," Gillian said. "Actual words. Then tell me what it commands and to whom."

John recited it, because he had memorized it years ago for a reason he no longer remembered. The words were about remembering, about keeping a day separate, and they were set in a passage about a people escaping slavery. Guneet pulled out his phone and found the surrounding verses, and for a while the three of them commandeered the entire table, pushing paper plates aside to lay out the text like a map. The uncle's card game dissolved behind them. Someone's cousin asked what they were doing and got no answer.

"Here's my problem," Gillian said. "You want the rule to be flexible because your family treats it flexibly. So when you read 'remember' and 'keep,' you'll find flexibility in it, because that's what you already believe. That's eisegesis. You're finding only what you brought."

"That's not fair," John said, but he said it slowly, because part of him recognized the shape of the accusation. He had done exactly that in his first draft, written two pages about how the spirit of the rule mattered more than the letter, without once quoting the letter.

He asked his grandmother for her old copy of the text, the one with the cracked spine, and she brought it out wrapped in a dish towel as though it were warm. She sat down at the end of the table without being invited, which was how she entered most rooms. John read the passage aloud again, this time from the book, and asked her what it meant when she was young.

"It meant the street went quiet," she said. "Everyone's street, not just ours. That part is gone. You cannot keep a quiet street alone."

Guneet wrote that down. Gillian looked skeptical, and John understood why: a memory of a quiet street was context, not command, and a debate judge would want the argument to turn on the words. But the words themselves were anchored in a story about freedom from labor, and the context was a whole community exiting slavery together, and John found that if he held those two things at once, the rule looked less like a private ritual and more like a public rhythm, something a cosmopolitan city of strangers might still have reason to want, whether or not they kept it the way his grandmother had.

"So what's your case?" Gillian asked. "Still applies, or doesn't?"

"Partially," John said. "The text ties the rule to release from work, and it's given to a community, not to individuals. So my position is that the obligation survives but shifts. It's on the society to protect the rest, not only on each person to observe it. What I can't settle is whether the text itself licenses that shift or whether I'm doing what you accused me of. That part stays open, and I'm going to say so at the tournament."

Gillian folded her flyer smaller and smaller until it was a hard little square. "You'll lose rounds with an honest 'I don't know' in the conclusion."

"Probably," John said.

His uncle appeared behind them with a tray of cups and, finding no room on the table, set it on his mother's book, which lay open to the passage they had been arguing over. Nobody moved it. He dealt himself into his card game, and his mother reached over and slid the tray aside, then closed the book gently, keeping her thumb in it as a bookmark, and went back to watching him play.

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: Modus ponens is the valid argument form 'if P then Q; P; therefore Q', and it is valid no matter what P and Q stand for.
story:
The group chat lit up at 11:42, four notifications in a row, and Jayden propped the phone against his water bottle so he could eat cereal and read at the same time. Angelique had sent a photo of the worksheet, Problem 6 circled twice in red ink, and beneath it: "this is due at 8am and I do not get it AT ALL." Skyla answered first, a wall of text about how she'd copied the answer off some homework site and the site had gotten it wrong too.

Jayden pulled the worksheet toward him across the kitchen table. Problem 6: If the train is late, then Marcus misses the meeting. The train is late. Therefore, Marcus misses the meeting. Valid or invalid? He'd written "valid" and moved on, but Angelique's circle and the red X through Skyla's copied answer made him feel like the floor had shifted under something he'd been standing on all week. He typed: "what did perez mark it."

"Valid," Angelique said. "Both of ours. He wrote 'see rubric' and I want to scream."

The kitchen smelled like toast going from golden to black; his father had sublimated his own stress about the mortgage into a campaign to fix the toaster, and now the toaster sat disassembled in a shoebox beside the sink. Jayden put his bowl down. He read the problem again, out loud, quietly, the way he did when nobody was home to hear him. If the train is late, then Marcus misses the meeting. The train is late. Something about it itched. It was obviously true, but obviously true the way a locked door is obviously a wall until you find the handle.

"Try this," he typed. "If the flurb is green, then the wug sings. The flurb is green. Therefore, the wug sings."

Skyla's reply came fast: "what is a flurb." Then: "wait." Then a full minute of nothing, the typing bubble appearing and vanishing like something surfacing and diving again. Angelique sent three question marks. Jayden sat back, the phone warm in his palm, his pulse doing something embarrassing for a Tuesday night over nonsense words. Because the flurb argument worked. It worked exactly as well as the train argument, and neither flurb nor wug meant anything at all, and that felt like being handed a key that fit every lock in the city.

"Valid," Skyla typed. "It has to be valid. Even though it's garbage."

"Right," Jayden typed, then deleted it, then retyped it. "The words don't matter. It's the shape." He remembered Mr. Pérez saying the name once, barely, in passing, something Jayden had filed away like a receipt he never expected to use: "It's called modus ponens," Pérez had said to the kid in the second row, and moved on. Jayden typed it into the chat. Angelique sent back: "ponens like a spell."

"It kind of is," he typed. "If P then Q, P, therefore Q. You can put anything in the blanks. Train, flurb, whatever. It stays valid."

The reversal arrived at 11:58, when Angelique sent a photo of the rubric Pérez had handed out, zoomed in on the third bullet: valid arguments may still have false conclusions if the premises are false. Below it she wrote: "so our problem 6 marked valid was RIGHT and the site's was wrong because the site said invalid?? or is he saying we can't tell if Marcus missed the meeting because we don't know if the train was actually late??" Jayden read it three times. He'd been so sure the argument's shape was the whole answer, but Angelique was staring at the gap between an argument being valid and it being true, and he couldn't close that gap from his kitchen table, not with the toaster in pieces and the clock climbing past midnight.

He tried to write it out. "The form is valid no matter what P and Q stand for," he typed. "But whether the conclusion's true depends on whether the premises are true. So the argument works even if the train's on time, it just gives you a false thing in a true shape. I think." He stared at "I think." He could hear Skyla's voice in the words, the way she'd push back tomorrow in class, canny and relentless, and he already knew she'd ask about the flurb: if the flurb isn't green, what does the argument do then, nothing? Everything? He didn't know. He had the shape and not the substance, and only one of those was due at 8 a.m.

Angelique was typing. The bubble pulsed. Jayden watched it, spoon forgotten, milk going cold in the bowl.

"Wait," she wrote. "Perez just posted. Test moved to Thursday."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Deliberate practice means working on specific weaknesses with a clear goal and immediate feedback, which improves skill more than simply playing through pieces already known.
story:
The auditorium smelled of dust and radiator paint, and Isabelle had the stage to herself for forty minutes before the others arrived. She set her case on the edge of the piano bench and opened it the way she always did, hinges first, like something might escape. She had been playing violin since she was nine, and for most of those years she had ended every practice the same way: with the Allemande, the one piece she could play from memory, her fingers moving before her mind caught up.

Mr. Sutherland came in through the side door with his coffee and his folder of photocopied excerpts. He had agreed to hear her once a week before school because the regional audition was in March, and because, she suspected, he felt sorry for anyone practising in an auditorium. He sat in the fourth row, where the acoustics were honest, and listened to the Allemande all the way through. When she lowered the bow he didn't clap, which was usual, and didn't smile, which was not.

"That's the third time I've heard that this week," he said. "Play me the Gavotte. Just the two bars before the repeat."

"They're the same two bars I got wrong on Tuesday."

"I know."

She raised the bow anyway and played the first bar, and the shift from third position to fifth landed a half-step flat, the note sitting in the hall like a coin dropped on marble. She stopped, went back, did it again. Flat again. On the third try she got the note but lost the rhythm, and on the fourth she got the rhythm and dropped the note, and she could feel her ears getting hot even though nobody was watching except a man drinking coffee in the dark.

"You played that Allemande beautifully," Mr. Sutherland said, "and it taught you nothing you didn't already know. You had a goal for those two bars, you got it wrong, and you heard it wrong right away. That's worth more than an hour of what you already play well. There's a name for that, working on a specific weakness with a clear goal and feedback you can hear immediately. It improves skill more than playing through pieces you already know."

"Deliberate practice," Isabelle said, because her brother had a book about it on the kitchen table all last summer, and she had flipped past it on her way to the porch with her violin.

"That's the word," he said, and finished his coffee.

She thought about protesting that the Allemande was what made her want to play at all, that there had to be room in a life for the thing you were already good at, but she didn't say it, because she suspected he would agree, and then she would have nothing to argue with. Instead she went back to the two bars. She slowed them to half speed. She played only the shift, the slide of one finger up the string, twenty times, listening each time for the coin-on-marble sound that meant she'd missed. On the nineteenth try the note came out round and warm, and something in her chest loosened, the way a room feels different when a window opens.

The auditorium doors banged and Luc came in with his trumpet case and a bag of pastries, early for the brass sectional. He wanted the pastries to be for two people, which they always were, and he wanted, more delicately, to ask her to play the duet at the spring concert, which he had failed to ask about three times since December. She could see the question forming in him like weather.

"Listen to this," she said, before he could speak, and played the two bars at full speed. The shift landed. It landed again when she repeated it, and a third time, and she was grinning in a way that felt unfamiliar at this hour of the morning.

"You fixed that?" Luc said. "Maia said you'd been stuck on it since Christmas."

"I was stuck because I was practising the wrong thing. Or the right thing too many times." She hesitated, because the honest version was less tidy. She didn't know yet whether the two bars would hold under pressure, whether the note would survive an audition room with a table of judges and her own heartbeat in her ears. She knew only that this morning, in this hall, it had worked, and that she could not remember the last time a whole hour of the Allemande had changed anything. Both things were true and she refused to drop either one.

She put the violin down for a minute and took a pastry, and Luc leaned against the piano with his case still shut, working up to the duet the way a swimmer works up to cold water. "It's the Handel," he said finally. "The one for trumpet and violin. Mr. Sutherland already said the orchestra could do it if we had both parts."

"You've had the music since December."

"I was waiting until you fixed those bars. I didn't want you saying yes because you felt bad."

The auditorium was filling now with chairs scraping and the low murmur of the sectional gathering, and Mr. Sutherland had gone up to the lighting booth to argue with a switch. Isabelle looked at the two bars in her music, pencilled now with so many markings they were nearly black, and then at Luc, holding the Handel out flat across both palms like something breakable.

"Okay," she said. "But we rehearse the hard parts first, not the easy ones."

"Not even once through for fun?"

"Not even once." She took the music from him, and propped it open on the stand, and set her bow on the string at the fifth position, ready.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: An adjustable-rate mortgage's interest rate changes periodically with a market index, so its monthly payment can rise, unlike a fixed-rate mortgage's.
story:
The coffee can of screws came first, as it always did. Elliot had come to his grandfather's house to help clear the garage before the autumn sale, and the two of them spent the morning sorting hardware into jars while the radio murmured about interest rates. He liked this about the place, that a whole afternoon could be organized around small decisions, what to keep, what to price at a dollar, what to carry to the curb. At home his mother was composing an email to their landlord, and Elliot had read enough of it over her shoulder to know the words "security deposit" and "annual increase," phrases that seemed to belong to a language adults spoke fluently and he was only now beginning to hear.

Midway through the boxes, Ms. Pereira from next door appeared at the side door holding a casserole dish, which was her way of arriving anywhere. She and the grandfather talked over the fence about the hydro lines, and then she said something that snagged in Elliot's attention. Her mortgage payment had gone up that month, four hundred dollars, and nothing else had changed. Same house, same bank, same job. She said it like a complaint about weather, a thing that simply happened to a person.

"Nothing changed," Elliot said, when she had gone and they were back among the jars. "How can the payment change if nothing changed?"

His grandfather wiped his hands and looked at him with the particular pleasure of a man who has been waiting years for someone to ask. "Depends what kind she has," he said. "There's fixed-rate, and there's adjustable. Ours was fixed, thirty years, same payment every month of it. Adjustable, the rate changes every so often with the market. When the market goes, the payment goes." He did not expatiate further, which Elliot appreciated; the old man had a habit of turning any topic into a lecture, and this time he left the sentence sitting there like a jar waiting for its lid.

Elliot turned it over while he stacked. A fixed rate, then, was a kind of promise; an adjustable rate was a bet. You took the lower payment at the start and accepted that the market could move against you later, the way Ms. Pereira's had, or it could move for you, though she was not currently in a mood to consider that side of the wager. He texted Penelope, who had spent the summer working at a property management office and would know things. "Mortgage payment can just go UP?" he wrote. "If it's adjustable, yeah," she answered. "Mine would rent for the whole apartment. Whole different animal. Rent's set by the lease, and you put down a deposit you get back if you don't wreck the place. A house, you need a down payment first, five, ten, twenty percent of the price, and then you borrow the rest." She added a shrugging emoji, as if to say that money worked this way whether or not it seemed reasonable.

The percentages were what surprised him most. He had assumed, vaguely, that buying a house meant having a house's worth of money. Instead it meant having a fraction of it and promising the bank the rest over decades, at a rate that either never moved or moved with the market, depending on which kind of gamble you had chosen, or been talked into, or stumbled into. He tried to imagine explaining all this to Anabel, who was already at university and had once described credit cards as "free money with extra steps." He suspected she would call the whole system profligate by design, spending money nobody had on houses nobody could outright own, and he suspected she would be half right and half ungrateful, the way eighteen-year-olds usually were.

He looked up the terms that evening on the kitchen computer while his grandfather watched a baseball game he claimed not to care about. Fixed-rate, adjustable-rate, down payment, amortization, a word whose shape he liked. He found forum threads from 2008 full of people describing payments that had climbed past their wages, and other threads, quieter, from people whose adjustable rates had fallen and who felt lucky and slightly guilty about it. Which was it, then, prudence or luck? His grandfather had chosen fixed in 1987 and had been called cautious to the point of timidity by his own brother, who had chosen adjustable, done well for a decade, and then, after a stretch of what the family only ever called his recidivism with the racetrack, lost the house entirely. Caution and luck were not opposites so much as neighbours, and the fence between them was lower than anyone wanted to admit.

"Did you almost not make the down payment?" Elliot asked, carrying two teas into the den. "Back when you bought this place."

His grandfather muted the game. "Never had it," he said. "Your grandmother did. Her mother's insurance money, all of it, three thousand dollars in 1968. I signed the papers and moved in feeling like a tenant in my own marriage for the first year." He laughed at something in Elliot's face. "Everyone borrows from somebody, kid. Bank, mother, wife. The only difference is who raises the rate on you."

From the kitchen, Elliot's phone buzzed with a message from Penelope: "Also, heads up, your grandpa's neighbour just put in an offer on the Henderson place. Adjustable. Says the payments are cheaper."

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: An ad hominem argument attacks the person making a claim instead of the claim itself, and it is treated as a fallacy in formal debate.
story:
The kitchen table had become a country where Hannah did not live yet. Her notebook lay open to a page of Spanish phrases, her laptop balanced on a stack of cookbooks so the camera would catch her face instead of her ceiling, and on the screen Felix and Dereck were arguing about whether tap water counted as a prop.

"You have five minutes," Felix said, "and you're defending the carbon tax. In Spanish. Ready?"

"Give me one second." Hannah flattened the page. She had chosen the carbon tax because her father installed solar panels and talked about it at dinner until her mother changed the subject, and because Ms. Huang had said in class that you should argue something you half believe, so that winning did not feel like lying. That had seemed wise in October. Now, three days before the exchange debate with the school from Querétaro, it seemed like a trap she had set for herself.

She began. The first minute was clumsy, the way a first attempt always is, her consonants arriving in the wrong order, her subjunctive collapsing at the worst moments. But somewhere in the second minute the language stopped being a series of translations and started being a corridor she could walk down. She was making the point about pricing emissions honestly when Dereck interrupted her.

"Tu acento es terrible," he said, grinning, and then in English, "Sorry, sorry, keep going, but it's true, you sound like a robot ordering at a drive-thru."

Hannah stopped. She had a rebuttal prepared about regressive taxation and rebate cheques; she could feel it waiting in her mouth. Instead she heard herself say, in slow, careful Spanish, "Mi acento no es un argumento." The clock on the stove showed she had two minutes left.

"Wait," Felix said. "Hang on. That's the thing Ms. Huang drilled us on. Attacking the person instead of the point. Ad hominem." He snapped his fingers. "In formal debate it counts as a fallacy. Like, the judges will actually dock for it."

Dereck leaned back in his chair. "I wasn't making an argument. I was making a joke."

"Then it was a joke that looks exactly like an ad hominem," Felix said. "Which is worse, because a real opponent would do it on purpose."

Hannah wrote the word in her notebook, large, and underneath it, smaller, the sentence she had improvised. My accent is not an argument. She looked at it and something rearranged itself in her chest. All year she had treated her accent as a defect to be apologized for, practicing rolled r's in the bathroom mirror, cringing at recordings of herself. But the accent was not a flaw in her reasoning. It was just the sound of a person arriving from somewhere else. If an opponent mocked it, he would be telling the judges he had nothing to say about carbon pricing, and that was information she could use.

"Let's run it again," she said. "Dereck, be the guy from Querétaro. Mock me. Really commit."

"You want me to insult you."

"I want you to insult me so I can practice not caring in two languages."

They ran it four more times. Dereck found increasingly creative ways to suggest that a gringa from a town with one traffic light could not possibly understand environmental policy, and Hannah practiced the same response: acknowledge, redirect, return to the argument. "Es posible que mi acento te distraiga," she said on the fourth run. "Pero el precio del carbono no cambia con mi pronunciación." Felix clapped without making a sound, the way people applaud in libraries.

Afterward, when the boys had signed off and the kitchen was quiet, her father came down in his socks and asked how it went. She told him about the ad hominem, about Dereck's terrible robot impression, about the sentence she kept landing on.

"Good for you," he said. Then, because he was her father, "You know what you should also say tomorrow? That people who call the carbon tax radical are being reactionary. They treat any change as an attack."

"That's the thing, though," Hannah said, and pulled her notebook back toward her. "I can't just call them reactionary back. That's the same move. I'd be labeling the people instead of answering their argument." She tapped the page. "I have to historicize it instead. Show that we've priced other things before, sulfur in the nineties, and the world didn't end. Then their framing looks anachronistic, like they're arguing against a version of the debate that already finished."

Her father frowned. "Where'd you learn that?"

"Ms. Huang says it constantly. I only just understood it tonight."

He stood at the fridge for a while, holding the handle without opening it. "Your mother thinks I talk too much at dinner," he said finally. "Maybe she's right."

"She's half right," Hannah said. "You talk too much when I'm eating. But tomorrow you can talk all you want on the drive." She looked down at the notebook, at the word ad hominem and the sentence beneath it, and drew a small box around both, the way she marked things she intended to keep. Then she closed the laptop, carried her notes upstairs, and stood in front of the bathroom mirror, saying the sentence out loud, listening to her accent instead of fixing it.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: When parking facing downhill next to a curb, turning the front wheels toward the curb means the car will roll into the curb, not into traffic, if the brakes fail.
story:
The cones were still in the trunk of his mother's car from the night before, two of them wedged behind the spare tire, and Jaxon carried them out into the garage's driveway while Layan held the door. The garage belonged to Mr. Sharma, who had offered the wide apron of pavement every evening that week because it matched the dimensions of the test site downtown, or close enough. "Six metres between them," Layan said, laying a tape measure along the asphalt. "You said the handbook says six." She set the cones a hand's width further apart anyway, then moved them back, and Jaxon watched her measure twice, knowing she did it for him and saying nothing.

His test was at nine the next morning. What he wanted was simple and total: to pass, to drive himself to the campus in September, to stop arranging his life around the schedules of people with cars. But the wanting had split somewhere in the week, because Mr. Sharma kept telling him driving was a craft of small mercies toward strangers, and Lohan, who had passed in June, kept telling him the examiner wanted crispness, angles, a performance. "You're trying to codify a thing that's mostly nerve," Lohan had said from the porch on Wednesday, popping the tab on a can. Jaxon had laughed, and then had not, because he suspected they were both right and the two truths sat badly together.

He parallel parked eleven times that evening. On the twelfth, Mr. Sharma came out with his watering can, paused at the roses, and said, "Try it on the hill." The street outside rose in a long, gentle grade toward the traffic light, and there was a curb the whole way up. Jaxon pulled forward, reversed between a parked hatchback and a cardboard box Mr. Sharma set out as a second car, and eased to the kerb on the slope. He cut the wheel hard left, away from the curb, because that felt like the polite, careful thing, the small-mercies thing, and he sat there satisfied.

"Shut it off and come look," Mr. Sharma said, which was all he said. He did not come look himself. He went back to the roses.

Jaxon got out and stood at the curb, staring at his front wheels, angled out toward the road like they were pointing at the oncoming lane. Layan came around from the passenger side with the handbook already open, her thumb holding a page. "Here," she said, and read the line aloud. "When parking facing downhill next to a curb, turn the front wheels toward the curb. That way the car will roll into the curb, not into traffic, if the brakes fail." She looked up. "Downhill. You're facing downhill, right?"

He was. He crouched at the bumper and turned the wheel with his hand on the tire, watching the front wheels swing right, toward the curb, so that anything that slipped would slide sideways into concrete instead of out where a cyclist or a kid on a scooter would be. "I had it exactly backwards," he said. "I was trying to be careful and I aimed the car at the street."

Layan wrote it on the back of a grocery receipt in her looping hand, downhill, wheels to the curb, rolls into the curb not into traffic, and tucked it under the wiper so he would see it when they drove to the highway. Then they drove to the highway, because Mr. Sharma had insisted the merge counted for more than the park and could not be learned in a driveway. Lohan came along for the last hour, riding in back with a pugnacious energy, narrating gaps like a sports announcer, and Jaxon snapped at him once, short and ugly, before catching himself. "Sorry," he said, and Lohan said, "Take the next one anyway," and signaled, checked, matched speed, and slid into a gap between a delivery van and a sedan with room to spare.

At the top of the ramp Layan said, "You did that smooth," and Mr. Sharma, following in his own car to bring them home, flashed his lights twice, which Layan swore was a compliment. Jaxon held the lane, steady at the limit, and thought about the wheels turned toward the curb, about how being careful and being correct were not the same thing and he could not yet say what joined them. Maybe nothing did. Maybe you just had to hold both, like Mr. Sharma's mercy and Lohan's crispness, like a polity that only worked when its disagreeing members still signalled and let each other in.

They took the exit and looped back to the garage as the light failed. He parked on the hill one last time, facing downhill, and turned the front wheels toward the curb until he felt the tire kiss the concrete. Then he sat with his hands off the wheel, engine ticking, and Layan leaned over from the passenger seat and tapped the receipt under the wiper.

"Leave it for the morning," she said. "In case you're tired before you're nervous."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases enzymes that produce syn-propanethial-S-oxide, a vapor that irritates the eyes and makes them tear.
story:
The after-hours kitchen smelled like celery and burnt toast, and Jasmine had exactly ninety minutes before her father's shift ended and the soup had to be in the car, cooling in the lidded pot Mr. Watanabe had lent her for the third time that semester. Her father had worked doubles all month since her mother started the night course, and the agreement in their house was simple: whoever cooked did not have to clean. Jasmine wanted the cooking. She wanted the pot on the stove and the table set before anyone got home, because it was the one thing she could finish completely.

She laid out the onions on the steel counter, three of them, yellow and papery, the size of softballs. Chicken and rice soup, the recipe her grandmother had dictated over the phone in September, back when the calls still came weekly. Since the diagnosis, the calls were shorter, and the recipes arrived on scraps of paper in envelopes with her looping script gone small and careful. Tonight's envelope sat propped against the flour bin, and beside it her phone, face up, where her brother had already sent four messages.

Mr. Watanabe unlocked the storeroom and wheeled out the cutting boards, pausing at her station on his way past. "You're the last one, Jasmine. I'll be in my office grading, so call out if the burner acts up." He had let her use the classroom kitchen on Thursday evenings all fall, on the condition that she left it cleaner than she found it. He never asked why she needed it, which she appreciated, because the answer involved a stove at home that sparked and a landlord who had been promising to fix it since August.

She halved the first onion and began to chop, and within a minute her eyes were burning and streaming. She wiped them on her sleeve and kept cutting, but by the second onion she had to stop, blinking at the ceiling, tears sliding down to her jaw. The phone buzzed. Her brother, home alone with his own dinner of toaster waffles, had apparently decided to check on her progress: a photo of the soup recipe's envelope, then the words, "hope it tastes like grandma's," and then, when she sent back a selfie with red eyes and wet cheeks to explain the delay, the reply came fast: "you're CRYING? over SOUP? lmaooo."

She remonstrated with him in type, thumbs hammering: I am not crying, it is the onions, every single time you have ever cooked you would know this except you have never cooked anything. He answered with a single crying-laughing emoji, and she put the phone face down and went back to the board, sniffling, furious, and, underneath the fury, stung in a way she did not want to examine. It felt like he was laughing at the whole project, at the idea that she could stand in for a grandmother whose hands had made this soup for forty years.

Paula and Eleni came in at six, as arranged, because the recipe said to serve six and her family was only three. Paula took one look at Jasmine's face and gasped with delight rather than alarm. "What happened? Are you okay?" Eleni, who had her tablet tucked under her arm the way other people carried keys, was already peering at the onion halves with her glasses pushed up into her hair. "Wait, wait, this is the thing," she said, tapping at the screen. "Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases enzymes that produce syn-propanethial-S-oxide. It's a vapor. It irritates your eyes and makes them tear. That's all it is. It's not you, it's chemistry."

Jasmine read the screen twice, blinking through the last of the sting. A vapor. A compound with a name long enough to be a small archipelago of syllables floating between her and her brother's teasing. She picked up the phone and typed it out slowly, carefully, copying the word letter by letter: it's called syn-propanethial-S-oxide, it's a vapor that irritates your eyes, and you are a congenital pest. Her brother replied, "congenital???" and then, a minute later, "ok that's actually kind of cool. make extra for me."

Paula was already peeling carrots at the sink, having appointed herself prep cook without discussion, and Eleni set the tablet on the shelf above the stove and started reading the grandmother's recipe aloud in a wobbly imitation of an old-country accent that made Paula laugh so hard she nearly grated her thumb. The soup came together in stages, the onions going translucent and sweet into the oil, the garlic following, then the stock, then the rice measured out in the chipped cup from the storeroom that Mr. Watanabe claimed was older than the school itself. Jasmine stirred and tasted and added salt, and found herself telling the girls about the phone calls shrinking, and how she had been afraid the soup would taste like grief, like a thing made only because someone might not be around to make it much longer.

"That's a lot to put on an onion," Paula said, which was Paula's way, blunt and warm at once. Eleni said nothing, only stirred the pot and then held out the spoon, and Jasmine tasted again and found that it tasted like chicken and rice and dill, like a Saturday afternoon, like being eleven and standing on a stool. It tasted like the soup. That was all, and it was somehow enough.

At seven twenty Mr. Watanabe emerged from his office with his coat already on, sniffed the air appreciatively, and wrote her a late pass for the building's back door. The pot went into a milk crate lined with a towel, and Jasmine carried it out to the car with the envelope of her grandmother's handwriting pressed flat against her chest, the plastic sleeve fogging faintly with the heat coming up through the lid. Paula and Eleni followed with the bowls and the bread, and the three of them stood in the dark parking lot for a moment, breath steaming, waiting for her father's headlights to swing in past the chain-link fence.

When the car pulled up, her brother was in the passenger seat, grinning, holding his phone out the window with the photo of her red-eyed selfie already displayed. Jasmine set the pot on the roof of the car, unlocked the trunk, and said, "Say the word, and you get seconds." He squinted at her. "The which?" "Syn-propanethial-S-oxide," she said, lifting the lid so the steam rose between them. "Say it, and hand me the bowls."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Acrylic paint is water-based while wet, but it dries quickly and becomes water-resistant once dry.
story:
The art shed smelled of pine sap and wet wool, and Logan had claimed the corner table by the window because the light there made the glaze on his tiles look almost liquid. He was building a mosaic, twelve clay squares he had fired in the camp kiln the week before, and he wanted a river running across all twelve, a grey-blue vein that would hold the whole thing together. The problem was that acrylic, his chosen medium, would not stay put. It dried on the palette before he could blend it, and when he tried to thin it again, the paint refused him, beading on the surface like water on wax.

He had his suspicions by the third morning. When the paint was fresh, it answered to his brush and to the cup of water he kept beside him; he could wash it off his fingers, dilute it to a wash, drag it across the clay in layers. But leave it even through a lunch break and it hardened into something the water could not touch. "It's water-based while it's wet," he said aloud, mostly to the tiles, "and water-resistant once it's dry." He turned the words over, testing them against what his hands had already shown him. So that was the rule. Work fast, or lose the paint.

He was not the only one losing paint. Makayla, two tables over, had left her brushes lying on a bench during the swim block, and when she came back with her hair still dripping, the bristles had stiffened into a single grey blade. She bent one and it snapped at the ferrule, and her face went very still, the way it did when she was deciding whether something counted as a catastrophe. The brushes belonged to her grandmother. Logan knew this because he had been there in February, in Makayla's basement, when she had unpacked the old wooden case and shown him the sable rounds her grandmother had used for thirty years of watercolors.

That afternoon he took the ruined brushes to Ms. Hoffmann, who ran the art program and kept a shelf of rescue supplies behind the drying rack. She did not lecture him about acrylic or its habits. She set out a jar of brush cleaner and a basin of warm water and said only, "Sit. Soak them. Some of the hairs may come back." So he sat, on an overturned milk crate, holding the brushes under the water like a man baptizing small birds, while the dried acrylic softened at its own pace and clouded the basin grey.

Duncan found him there an hour later and dropped onto the crate beside him. "You trying to exonerate yourself for the swim block?" Duncan asked. "You weren't even on the dock." Logan flexed one of the brushes against his palm; the bristles moved together now, stiff but together. "They're hers," he said. "Her grandmother's. I'm just the one who saw it happen." Duncan peeled the label off a bottle of cleaner and rolled it into a tight cylinder. "She's not mad at you, man. She's mad at the paint." It was, Logan thought, a distinction that mattered more than Duncan knew. Makayla had not blamed anyone; she had simply gone quiet and carried the case out of the shed with both hands, as though it were something wounded.

He worked the last brush free of the hardened acrylic, gently, combing the hairs apart with a pin, and thought about the way the paint had behaved all week. There was something almost honest about it. It offered you everything while it was wet, complete surrender to the brush and the water, and then it closed itself off, sealed its color inside a skin that no one could get through again. Not exactly an encapsulation, since the pigment was the same throughout, but the effect was similar: a moment of openness, then a door shutting. His parents were in the middle of exactly that kind of moment, one of those summers when the house had two separate weathers in it, and he had been treating their silence like his palette, assuming he could come back after lunch and everything would still be workable.

At supper he carried the cleaned brushes in their case across the picnic area and set them on the bench beside Makayla's tray. She opened the case slowly. Three of the five had recovered fully; one kept a slight bend; one would never hold a point again. She ran her thumb along the hairs of the best one and did not say anything for a while, and Logan did not fill the space, because he had learned this summer that some silences were wet paint and some were dry, and you had to know which before you touched them.

"I'm doing the river again tomorrow," he said finally. "From the start, fast, no breaks. You want to lay the blue?" Makayla looked up at him, the brush still in her hand, and across the lake the sun was going down behind the black ridge of the hills, the rocks there looking flat and dark as something igneous, poured out of the earth long ago and cooled into its permanent shape. She closed the case with a soft click. "Bring two water cups," she said. "We're not leaving anything out in the air again."

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: In the United States, a 100-year flood zone does not mean a flood every 100 years; it means the area has a 1 percent chance of flooding in any given year.
story:
Lauren found the house listing at eleven at night, tucked in an email from her uncle with the subject line "TOO GOOD TO BE TRUE?" and a photo of a squat beige bungalow beside a creek. The price was the thing. In a neighborhood where everything else started with a six, this one began with a two, and the listing's final line read, like a taunt, "Located outside the floodpath for a full century!" She screenshotted it and brought it to school the next morning, because that semester she was taking Mr. Xu's elective in geographic information systems, where for three weeks she had been learning to stack city data like pancakes.

The lab smelled like dry-erase markers and the vending machine's idea of coffee. Mr. Xu had given them a project with no ceiling on it: overlay the city's flood risk layer on the housing layer and find something the two maps said together that neither said alone. Lauren had been morose about it for days, convinced that maps of anything were just bureaucrat coloring books, until she saw the phrase "full century" in a real estate listing and felt something click sideways in her brain.

She dropped into the seat beside Angelica, who was already zoomed in on her own screen. "Okay," Lauren said, "hypothetical question." Angelica kept typing. "Is it a hypothetical about the beige house you've mentioned four times since Tuesday?" "It's a hypothetical about statistics," Lauren said, with dignity, and pulled up the FEMA layer, watching the hatched blue-green blotch bloom across the eastern half of the city.

Kaelen leaned over from the next row, chewing a pen cap. "You know those zones are political, right? They draw them to tank property values where they want." He said it with the cheerful certainty of someone who had read one forum thread at two in night before. Lauren dragged the bungalow's address into the search bar and watched the parcel snap into view, sitting square inside the hatched blotch like an egg in a nest.

"So it's in the zone," Angelica said. "But the seller says it's safe for a hundred years. A hundred-year zone. That's the term, right? It's literally called a 100-year flood zone." Lauren nodded slowly, the way she did when a math problem was about to turn inside out. "That's what it's called," she said. "But that's not what it means." She pulled up the plain-language FEMA page she'd found at midnight, squinting at it, then at the map, then back. "It means a one percent chance in any given year. Not one flood per century. One percent. Every year. Fresh dice every year."

Kaelen's pen cap stopped moving. "Wait. So over thirty years, a mortgage-length time, you're rolling that one percent thirty times." "I'm not allowed to do that math," Lauren said, "because the fact is just the one percent per year, and I don't want to extrapolate past what I actually know." Angelica snorted. "Since when are you the epistemology police?" "Since the beige house," Lauren said. "Also, can we talk about how 'clemency' is a weird word for a dry month? Because I've decided the weather owes me clemency after last Saturday."

The twist arrived by way of Mr. Xu, who wandered past their row, looked at Lauren's screen for exactly four seconds, and said, "Nice overlay. Did you check the year the map was revised?" She hadn't. The metadata, when she opened it, showed the flood layer had been updated after a remapping study, and the hatched zone now swallowed a stretch of creek-side street that older listings, including her uncle's, still cheerfully described as outside it. The house wasn't just in the zone. It was in the zone by newer math than the seller's claim, and the claim had been wrong about the zone even before it was wrong about the century.

Kaelen, to his credit, changed course like a sailboat. "Okay, so the lines aren't political," he said, peering closer. "Or, fine, maybe they're political and correct. Both can be true. But look at this part." He traced the housing layer's tax-assessment colors over the flood hatching, and where the two overlapped, the parcels went pale, cheap, dense. It was a lopsided geography, and it underpinned the whole "too good to be true" price in a way no single map had shown her. "So the cheap houses are sitting in the risky places," Angelica said quietly. "Which means the people who can least afford a flood are the ones getting the one percent roll."

Lauren wrote her uncle a long email in the lab, then deleted the long version and sent three sentences: the house is inside the 100-year flood zone, that means a one percent chance of flooding in any given year, and the seller's century claim is a misunderstanding of the term, at best. Then she added a screenshot, red circle drawn with a slightly crooked hand, because she wanted him to see the nest for himself. She hesitated over the send button, aware that she was telling a grown man what to do with his money based on a high school elective and one very hatched map.

Mr. Xu stopped behind her on his final lap of the room. "Nervous?" he asked. "A little," Lauren said. "I know what the map says. I don't know what he should do about it. Those feel like different questions." Mr. Xu shrugged, almost cheerful. "That's the whole field, kid. Now you know why we don't just hand people maps and go home." Lauren hit send, and beside her, Kaelen slid his chair over and said, "Show me how you did the layer stack. And then show me how to red-circle something, because my aunt is house hunting too."

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: The Keeling Curve zigzags every year because Northern Hemisphere plants take in carbon dioxide as they grow in spring and summer, then release it as leaves die and decay in autumn and winter.
story:
My grandfather's kitchen table had one leg shorter than the others, so every time I set my laptop down, the Keeling Curve tilted and I had to slide a folded napkin under the corner to level the world out. That is the kind of detail people forget, and I have decided not to forget it. I was there to explain greenhouse gases, out loud, in plain words, because Mr. Hoffmann had told me that if I couldn't explain something to my grandmother, I didn't understand it. He said it kindly, which made it worse. My grandparents had gone to bed early, and the house was so quiet I could hear the refrigerator thinking.

The assignment was simple enough on its face. Certain gases in the atmosphere let sunlight through and hold on to the heat that radiates back from the surface, so the planet warms more than it otherwise would. I could say that. I had said it, in class, and Mr. Hoffmann had nodded the way you nod at a parrot. The graph was the harder part: a line climbing across decades, measured at a place called Mauna Loa. Carbon dioxide, rising. I understood the rising. What I did not understand, and what nobody had bothered to tell me, was why the line zigzagged, sawtooth, tooth after tooth, all the way up. I assumed, with the confidence of someone who has never had to defend an assumption, that the instruments were old and the wiggles were noise. Errors. I planned to say so.

I called Janie first, because Janie answers her phone even at eleven at night, and because she had already done her presentation and would want to be magnanimous about it. She was magnanimous. She was also, I thought, being deliberately vague, the way she got when she wanted me to arrive at things myself so she could valorize my effort afterward, tell me I'd really grown, which I found condescending and also, when I was honest, occasionally deserved. "Look at the spacing of the wiggles," she said. "What comes around every year?" I said the cleaning schedule at the observatory. She hung up on me, gently.

Malia did not hang up. Malia, who was at her own grandmother's that week, a coincidence I keep meaning to examine, put her phone camera up to her own printout of the same graph. "Okay," she said, "forget the instrument. What happens to trees each season?" There was a window behind her with a dark yard in it, and a porch light making a small yellow stage of the grass.

I told her trees grow. She waited. I told her they lose their leaves. She waited longer, which is Malia's entire pedagogical method. Somewhere in that waiting, with the graph tilted on the bad table and my grandfather's almanac open beside it to a page about when to plant, the thing assembled itself in my head with an almost physical click. In spring and summer, plants grow, taking in carbon dioxide. In autumn and winter, leaves die and decay, releasing it back. The whole Northern Hemisphere breathing in and out, once a year, and the line at Mauna Loa recording the breath. Not errors. Seasons.

"It's the plants," I said. "Half the planet inhales and the line dips; then the leaves die and it climbs again, over and over, on top of the bigger climb." "There you go," Malia said, and ate something crunchy, and asked whether I was still coming Saturday, and I said I was, which I honestly intended.

Here is what I have to be careful about, because I have a habit of sanding my memories smooth until they say what I prefer. I did not understand it instantly. I sat at that table for another while, checking the timing against what my grandfather had taught me years ago about his own garden, his peas and his late tomatoes, and I noticed that the dips and peaks lined up with growing and dying, not with anything an instrument would do. But I still could not have said, with certainty, why the overall line climbs as steeply as it does, beyond the general story about gases holding heat and the things people burn. Mr. Hoffmann wanted certainty and I was going to give him the part I had and no more, which felt, for once, like honesty rather than laziness.

My grandmother came down for water at midnight and found me with the napkin and the tilted laptop. She asked what I was looking at, and I told her the whole thing, the gases, the sawtooth line, the hemisphere inhaling every spring and exhaling every fall, and she said, "So the earth is breathing," and I said yes, that was exactly it, and she stood in the doorway holding her glass and considering the idea the way she considered everything, as if it were ductile, able to be bent without breaking.

She said the maple out back would be turning soon, and then she went up to bed, and I left the graph on the screen, sawtooth and rising, while the maple stood outside in the dark, doing its part.

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: Frozen food can be thawed safely in the refrigerator, in cold water or in the microwave, but not by leaving it out on the counter.
story:
The schedule Mr. Carvalho taped to the walk-in door had Rebecca's name on it six times, which meant she had committed to something she only half understood. He ran the kitchen of a small Portuguese restaurant with the gravity of a much larger one, and when he'd caught her eating cold noodles from a container at 11 p.m. before a shift, he had declared, in front of the whole line, that a person who could not feed herself on a Tuesday was a person who had surrendered. So now she was learning: plan the week, write the list, shop once, cook in batches on Sunday, portion it all into labeled containers. He called it "running your own small restaurant with one customer." Charlie called it "Rebecca's era of sad little tubs," but Charlie had also eaten three of the tubs, so Rebecca felt her position was defensible.

The first Sunday she cooked five chicken thighs, a pot of rice, a tray of roasted vegetables, and a vat of black beans that boiled over while she was texting Rocco, so that part of the plan became "wipe the stove" instead of "lunch on Thursday." Mr. Carvalho had made her write the plan out like a prep list, in pencil, with a column for what could be frozen. Half the containers went into the restaurant's spare freezer because her mother's freezer at home was full of unidentifiable bags from an era best not investigated.

On Wednesday she was mesmerized by how well it was all working. She had packed Tuesday's beans and rice, eaten them on a bench between school and her shift, and felt, for the first time in months, like a person with infrastructure. She even wrote a message to Charlie about it, because Charlie had been skeptical in a way that deserved a written response.

Dear Charlie, it began. I know you said my Sunday afternoon of "cooking like a divorced dad" was the saddest thing you'd ever witnessed. I want you to know I ate a real dinner last night at an actual table, and this morning I was early to class instead of eating a granola bar on the stairs. Also, Rocco owes me a dollar because he bet the beans would kill someone and everyone is alive. Sincerely, a functioning adult. P.S. If you steal Thursday's container again I will become an autocrat about the fridge at home and you know I'll do it.

The problem came Thursday. Thursday's container was in the freezer at the restaurant, and Wednesday's shift had run late, and somewhere between the last table and the bus, Rebecca forgot the one instruction that had been circled on Mr. Carvalho's schedule: move tomorrow's meal down to the refrigerator the night before. She realized it at 7 a.m. on Thursday, standing in the walk-in, holding a solid brick of frozen chicken and rice with the label facing her like an accusation. Her first instinct was the obvious one, set it on the counter by the prep station and let the warm kitchen do the work. The kitchen was full of counter space and she was going to be there until six anyway.

She was reaching for the counter when Rocco came in to start the bread. He glanced at the container in her hand, then at the counter, and said, "Carvalho will end you." Rocco was mostly a joker, but he had a saturnine streak that surfaced at exactly the right moments, and this was one of them. He told her he'd been through this with the chef already, in his first month. The safe ways were three, and he counted them on flour-dusted fingers: the refrigerator, which took planning she had already failed at; cold water, which worked faster if you kept the food sealed and changed the water; and the microwave, which was fastest and slightly undignified. What you did not do, ever, was leave it sitting out on the counter, which Rocco said was the one thing Carvalho treated like a crime, worse than burning the garlic.

Rebecca stood there weighing it. The refrigerator way needed tomorrow, and it was already today. The cold water way meant a bowl in the sink and attention she'd have to pay between lunch prep and the dinner rush. The microwave meant five minutes and a slightly rubbery edge to the rice, eaten standing up before her shift, which was more or less the cold noodles problem in a new costume. She thought about how the whole point of the plan was to stop improvising, and how here she was, improvising again, except that this time she had three real options instead of one bad one. That felt like progress, even if it looked like a girl holding a frozen brick at seven in the morning.

She took the sealed container to the sink, found the biggest metal bowl, and ran the cold water. She set a timer on her phone for thirty minutes so she'd remember to dump it and refill, and she taped a note to the rim of the bowl that said Rocco's dollar, because he had earned it. Then she wrote a new line in pencil on Mr. Carvalho's schedule, under Thursday, where he would be sure to see it: "Thursday's meal thawed in cold water, per the three safe ways. Counter was considered and rejected."

When Mr. Carvalho came in at ten and read it, he stood in front of the walk-in door for a long moment, tapping the paper with one finger. "Cold water," he said finally. "Good. Tomorrow you move it the night before."

"Tomorrow I move it the night before," Rebecca said, and went to check the bowl.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Canada's first food bank opened in Edmonton on January 16, 1981.
story:
Anthony's mother had signed him up before he could argue, four hours on a Saturday, and the address she texted him turned out to be two doors down, the green house with the crooked fence where Ms. Szabó lived. He stood on his own front lawn in the glacial January wind and looked at it for a moment, at the garage door rolled up and the folding tables already set out under fluorescent light, and then he walked over because it was too cold to keep standing still.

"Perfect timing," Ms. Szabó said. She was shorter than he remembered from the street, quicker too, moving between crates of pasta and cans with an economy that made him feel large and useless. "Gloves are in the box. You're sorting dry goods, then bagging. Ashley is in the back."

Ashley was crouched over a bin of dented cans, holding each one up to the light like a jeweller. "Hey," she said, not looking up. "We have to check for bulging. Botulism. It's in the training sheet, apparently." She handed him a photocopy, soft at the folds, and at the bottom of the second page he found a paragraph headed "A Short History." He read it twice.
