Canada's first food bank had opened in Edmonton on January 16, 1981. Forty-odd years, which was less than his parents had been alive. Somehow he had assumed the things were permanent, like libraries, like hospitals, a fixture that had simply always been there because people had always needed them.

"They're not even fifty years old," he said. "Food banks. In the whole country."

Ashley shrugged. "Everything's younger than you think." She set aside a can of chickpeas with a seam of rust along the rim.

The morning took shape around him. Clients came through the garage at a pace Ms. Szabó seemed to know by feel, some quiet, some chatty, one woman who wanted to argue about the fairness of the tea selection. Anthony learned the system in pieces: intake at the clipboard, dry goods here, produce whatever the supermarket drop-off had brought, dairy in the cooler. He was bad at it at first, putting rice where the pasta went, and then less bad, and then there was a rhythm, and he stopped thinking about himself at all, which was, he suspected, the point of the whole exercise.

It was during a lull that Cristiano came in.

Anthony knew him from calculus, knew the way he leaned back in his chair and answered before the teacher finished the question, the kind of confidence that in a weaker person would have made him an autocrat but in Cristiano was mostly performance. Cristiano did not lean back now. He stood at the clipboard with his hood up, filling in his name in small careful letters, and he did not look at Anthony at all, and Anthony did not look at him either, and both of them pretended very hard that this arrangement was natural.

He thought of his father, suddenly, of a night two winters ago when the plant had cut its second shift and his old man sat at the kitchen table with a folder of applications and said nothing for an hour, and his mother made tea nobody drank. They had managed. There had been no garage two doors down in that version of events, no folding tables, and it occurred to Anthony that the difference between his family and Cristiano's had not been character or effort. It had been luck, and timing, and maybe somebody's willingness to swallow a certain amount of pride. His father would rather have gone hungry than be seen at a table like this. Anthony had always read that as dignity. Now, sorting cans beside a boy who was doing exactly that, being seen, he understood it might also have been something closer to shame, and that the two could wear the same coat.

He bagged Cristiano's order himself. Rice, pasta, two tins of tomatoes, the good bread that had come in that morning. He worked slowly and said nothing about the calculus homework, nothing about Friday, nothing about anything, and when he handed the bag across the table Cristiano took it with both hands and said, quietly, "Thanks, man," and there was no irony in it at all, which was the strangest part.

At four o'clock Ms. Szabó locked the cooler and gave him a paper cup of terrible coffee, and they stood in the doorway watching the street go blue with evening. He wanted to say something about January 16, 1981, about Edmonton, about how the whole country had got along without this until barely before he was born and what that meant about everything that came before and everything that might come after, but he could not make it come out as anything but a speech. He had spent the afternoon atoning for something, he realized, or trying to, some debt he couldn't name, and four hours of rice bags didn't expiate it, and she probably knew that better than he did.

"So you'll come back Saturday?" Ms. Szabó said.

The wind moved the flyer taped inside the garage door, the one with the history paragraph, and its edge lifted and settled. "Yeah," Anthony said. "I'll come back."

She took his cup and went inside, and he walked the two doors home under the streetlight with his hands deep in his pockets, and through the green house's window he could still see the folding tables, waiting.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: Percent yield is the actual mass of product obtained divided by the theoretical yield, multiplied by 100.
story:
The crystals were supposed to be blue, and they were, mostly, in the way that a bruise is mostly skin. Xavier held the jar up to the kitchen light while Alissa, on his phone propped against the sugar bowl, leaned closer to her own camera than anyone should lean to anything.

"They're supposed to be a gram and a half," she said. "The handout said so. Mine are a gram and nine hundredths. Where did the rest go?"

"Into the universe," Xavier said. "The universe keeps a lot of things."

The kitchen was his for the evening. His mother had taken his sister to swim practice, and the house had entered its usual interregnum between the after-school chaos and the return of everyone's claims on the stove. He had planned to spend it doing nothing in a disciplined, organized way, but Alissa had texted him a photograph of her science fair crystals at four o'clock with the single word "help," and here he was, dragging his chemistry binder out of his backpack like a man pulling a file for an audit he already knew he'd lose.

He had to transcribe the problem onto a fresh sheet of paper before it would mean anything, because his notes from class resembled a seismograph readout. Twelve grams of copper sulfate, molar mass two hundred forty-nine point seven, the equation balanced back in September by someone who had apparently understood September. He wrote it out, divided, multiplied by the mole ratio, came out with the answer that her handout had promised, and stared at it.

"So the math says a gram and a half," he said. "The scale says a gram point zero nine."

"Then the math is wrong."

"The math is never wrong. That's its whole personality."

On the counter behind him, his father's aquarium hummed, its lone surviving fish, a silver thing his father called "the pelagic one" with total inaccuracy, since it had never known anything larger than twenty gallons, drifting past the glass like a commuter who had missed the last train and accepted it. Xavier watched it for a second. It had also not become what it was supposed to become, and nobody was grading it.

Hussein arrived at six with his own binder and half a bag of chips, because Hussein did not believe in problems being solved on an empty stomach. His want was simpler than Alissa's and he stated it at the door: he needed the same material understood by Monday, and he intended to get it from whoever in this house had made the most progress, which by default meant Xavier, a state of affairs Hussein found hilarious enough to mention twice.

"You're the one who wrote 'probably' next to his last test answer," Hussein said, settling onto a stool.

"I stand by probably. It was a probabilistic situation."

They worked backward from the gram and a half, and then forward from the gram point zero nine, and Hussein, chewing, was the one who found the page in the textbook's back pages, the small paragraph Alissa's handout had buried under three bullet points. He read it aloud, slowly, the way he read everything, as though the words might try to escape.

"Percent yield is the actual mass of product obtained, divided by the theoretical yield, times one hundred."

Xavier wrote it down. Actual over theoretical, times one hundred. He plugged in her numbers, one point zero nine over one point five, and got seventy-two point seven.

"Seventy-two percent," he said. "You got seventy-two percent of what you were owed."

Alissa squinted at her own jar through the phone. "Is that bad?"

"It's not good. But now you have a number to be disappointed in, instead of a feeling."

She wanted, he understood over the next ten minutes, not a rescue but a defense. The science fair was Thursday, and her real question was whether she could stand in front of the gymnasium and tell the judges she'd made crystals that underdelivered, or whether she should remake the whole batch tonight and hope for bluer, heavier ones. Xavier, who had exactly one evening's authority on the subject, was in no position to grant it, and said so, and Hussein said that was the most honest thing anyone had told her all week.

They calculated what a perfect batch would have weighed, and what hers weighed, and whether the difference fit inside a plausible percent yield or a catastrophic one, and Xavier held two thoughts at once without collapsing them into one: that Alissa's crystals were a failure by the textbook's arithmetic, and that they were real, glassy, faintly blue, sitting in a jar on her desk while seventy-two percent was still a number somebody had bothered to measure. He did not know which thought he'd defend at the fair, if it came to that.

"So do I remake them?" Alissa asked.

The fish drifted past the glass again, unbothered, silver, short of the sea by any measure.

"Bring the jar," Hussein said, reaching for another chip. "Judges love a jar."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Kwanzaa, created by Maulana Karenga in 1966, runs from December 26 to January 1 and honors seven principles, one each day, beginning with Umoja, meaning unity.
story:
Gavin stood at the door of the cultural center with a paper cup of ginger punch in one hand and his phone in the other, scrolling through search results that all said the same thing in slightly different fonts. His aunt had cornered him twenty minutes ago by the coat rack. You're up after the drummers, she'd said. Second night, young man explains the principle. Except it wasn't the second night, it was the first, which meant Gavin had exactly the length of one drum performance, maybe four minutes, to become an authority on something he'd mostly absorbed through osmosis at this same hall for the past nine years.

He found Marylou by the stage, where she was taping down a cable that someone had already tripped over twice. She worked at the center part time, which meant she knew where the good chairs were and which punch bowl had the punch that wasn't mostly melted ice.

"I need you to fact check me in ninety seconds," he said. "Kwanzaa was created by Maulana Karenga, right, in 1966."

"Your aunt roped you into the principle speech." She wasn't asking. "Santino got the history table. He's over there trying to make a poster about the Black Arts Movement look like he didn't make it during lunch."

Gavin looked. Santino was indeed crouched beside a folding table, holding a marker in his teeth while he smoothed a piece of paper that had already begun to curl at the corners, an act of defiance against the laws of humidity. The hall itself had filled with the particular warmth of a December evening crowd: elders in chairs near the front, kids weaving between knees, the smell of fried plantains drifting from the back where the food tables were, Ms. Girma from the library arranging books on a display stand with the precision of a magistrate laying out evidence, each spine squared to the table's edge.

The drummers were finishing. Gavin's aunt caught his eye from across the hall and pointed at the microphone stand with the cheerful ruthlessness of a game show host.

"Okay," he said to Marylou, walking fast. "So it runs from December 26 to January 1. Seven nights. One principle a night, and tonight's the first one, which is the unity one. Umoja. That's all correct?"

"That's correct," Marylou said. "You'll be fine. Just don't start with 'webster's defines.'"

The drummers took their bows to a wall of applause, and suddenly the microphone was there and so was Gavin, facing a room that included his grandmother, two of his teachers, and a toddler who was currently eating a napkin. He took a breath.

"So I found out today that Kwanzaa was created by Maulana Karenga in 1966," he said, and heard his own voice sound steadier than expected off the back wall. "It runs from December 26 to January 1, seven days, and each day honors a different principle. One per day." He paused, and in the pause he noticed he actually had something to say, which was a novel experience during public speaking. "There are seven of them because it's not one idea, it's a week of them, and tonight is the first. Umoja. It means unity."

He hadn't planned the next part, but it came anyway. "I looked up the other six this afternoon, and some of them I'd heard my whole life without knowing they had names. And I was thinking, the reason there's a first day at all, a starting principle, is maybe that unity isn't automatic. Like, you can't exactly decree it. My mom and my uncle didn't speak to each other for three years over a car. A car. And what I noticed is that the argument calcified, it got hard and fixed, way before either of them could remember what it was originally about. Nobody wanted to be the one to soften first."

There was a ripple of laughter from the adult section, the specific laughter of people who knew exactly which car.

"Anyway." Gavin found his grandmother in the front row. She was not laughing; she was nodding slowly, which was worse and better at once. "I don't have a lesson. I just know that tonight everybody in this room drove here in the rain to sit next to each other, and tomorrow night there's a different principle, and we could do it again. That seems like the whole point of starting with Umoja. You get seven tries."

He stepped back from the microphone before it could develop feedback, and the applause was warm and ordinary, and Marylou gave him a thumbs up that was probably thirty percent sincere.

Afterward, near the plantains, Santino appeared beside him holding his rescued poster, one corner now weighted down with a cup. "Nice speech. You said calcified. Very deleterious vocabulary."

"That's not what deleterious means."

"It could be."

Ms. Girma passed by with an empty punch bowl and paused. "There's a young man at the library every January who asks for the Kwanzaa books after they've been put away," she said. "I'll set some aside for you this year, if you like." Then she moved on toward the kitchen, not waiting for an answer, because she never did.

Gavin looked out at the hall: his aunt already recruiting next year's victims, the toddler asleep in someone's lap with half a napkin still in hand, six more principles lined up across six more nights like unopened doors. His uncle, he noticed, had taken the chair beside his mother and was saying something to her over the noise.

"All right," Gavin said, and picked up a second plate. "Who made these plantains, because I need to have words."

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: The US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau notes a typical payday loan fee of $15 per $100 borrowed for two weeks equals an annual percentage rate of almost 400 percent.
story:
Aleah spread the eviction notice across the kitchen table next to Laurence's biology notes, smoothing the crease with the heel of her hand. Lane dropped into the third chair and set down two sodas from the corner store, the cans sweating rings onto the wood. Laurence's mother worked nights, so the kitchen belonged to them until eleven.

"I need four hundred by the first," Aleah said. "There's a place on Marsh Street. The cashier there said fifteen per hundred. That's it. Fifteen."

"Fifteen total?" Lane cracked her can.

"For two weeks. Then I pay back four sixty when my paycheck comes."

Laurence pulled her calculator out of her backpack, the cheap one with the cracked corner, the one she used for chemistry. She had been halfway through a worksheet on phenotypic variation in pea plants, and the numbers on the page blurred together with the ones Aleah was saying. She typed, deleted, typed again. "Wait. It's fifteen per hundred, every two weeks. A year is twenty-six of those."

"So?"

"So it's like fifteen, twenty-six times. On a hundred." She turned the calculator around. "The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says that's an annual percentage rate of almost four hundred percent."

Aleah took the calculator and looked at the screen as if the number might rearrange itself into something kinder. Four hundred. She had done the math herself on the bus, but only to the four sixty, only the two weeks, because two weeks was as far ahead as she could afford to think. Her mother would say pray on it. Her cousin would say everybody uses those places, that's what they're there for. Aleah set the calculator down between the sodas and the pea plant worksheet, and it sat there like something that had been dropped from a height.

"I can get the four hundred," Laurence said. "It's in my savings."

"No." Aleah's voice came out clipped. "No way."

"It's earning like nothing. One percent. Money just sits there."

"You're saving for the deposit on your dorm."

Laurence didn't answer. She was thinking that she wasn't being generous, exactly, that wanting to be thanked, wanting to be the one who solved it, made her something of an egoist, and that knowing that about herself didn't make the offer worse. She pushed the calculator aside. "Four hundred at four hundred percent APR, Aleah. You'd be paying them back all year. It would debilitate you before you even started college."

"I said no," Aleah said, but quieter.

Lane, who had been quiet through most of it, turned her phone around. On the screen was her bank app, a savings account her grandmother had started when she was nine. "Look. I put in twenty a month since I was twelve. It's not just what I put in anymore. The interest stacks on top of itself. Same thing, backwards." She slid the phone to the middle of the table next to the eviction notice, so that both of them were visible at once, the growth and the debt, the same principle running in opposite directions.

That was when the screen door clattered and Mr. Aquino leaned in from the porch, holding a casserole dish he'd brought back from the funeral luncheon, the one Laurence's mother had sent food to in March. He was the neighbor who fixed the fence and who told Laurence, whenever he saw her with a library book, that she read too much for her own good. He saw the notice on the table and didn't ask, just pulled the fourth chair out and sat down, setting the dish by the sodas.

"Marsh Street," he said. He tapped the edge of the paper. "That's where you were going."

"Maybe," Aleah said.

He didn't lecture. He took a pen from his shirt pocket and wrote nothing with it, just held it, and looked at the calculator, and looked at the phone with its small green number climbing, and waited the way adults wait when they've decided not to rescue anybody. Laurence recognized the tactic and almost smiled.

"There's the campus credit union," Lane said. "My brother got a small loan there. Real interest. Like nine percent."

"I'd need a parent to co-sign," Aleah said. "My mom can't."

"My mom could," Laurence said.

Aleah looked at her for a long moment. Behind them the fridge hummed, and Mr. Aquino uncapped his pen at last and wrote his own phone number on the corner of the eviction notice, under the landlord's, and pushed it across the table toward Aleah. "I do taxes for half the street," he said. "Call before you sign anything."

Aleah picked up the notice, folded it once, and put it in her jacket. Then she picked up the calculator too.

"I'm keeping this," she said. "I want to do the number again myself."

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: The Collingridge dilemma, from David Collingridge's 1980 book, says a technology's effects are hard to predict when it is new, but by the time they are clear it is hard to change.
story:
Nicolas opened the laptop at the kitchen table and logged into the school's new proctoring software, the one the district had bought over the summer. A small green circle appeared in the corner of his screen, and beneath it a line of text that read, somewhat redundantly, "Recording." He raised his hand to scratch his ear and watched the circle pulse, as though the program had an opinion about his hand.

The reason he was logged in at all was Mika. Two nights ago, during the algebra retake, the software had flagged Mika seventeen times for "suspicious gaze deviation," and Ms. Sutton had emailed a notice saying the flags would go on file. Mika swore he had only been looking at the ceiling, which he did when he was thinking, a habit everyone in their class could confirm. The appeal form was due Friday. Nicolas had told Mika he would help fill it out, partly because it was true and partly because Mika had a way of writing appeals that sounded like ransom notes.

Frederique joined the call from her room, her camera tilted toward a poster of a heron. "I found something," she said before Nicolas could say hello. "Other schools, same software. One district suspended forty kids in a week. Almost all of them were kids who didn't have a quiet room to test in. Siblings walking past. That kind of thing."

"So it's not just Mika being weird," Nicolas said.

"It's the software deciding what cheating looks like. And it looks like a boy with two little sisters."

Mika's window opened a moment later, audio crackling. "Is this the part where we say it's biased and everyone nods?"

"We could say it and then nobody nods," Frederique said. "That's what happened at the assembly."

Nicolas pulled up the appeal form. It wanted a written statement, three hundred words, explaining "the circumstances of the flagged session." He began typing, deleted it, and turned instead to a search bar. He wasn't sure what he was looking for until he found it: a scanned page from an old book, dense type, a 1980 copyright. The author's name was David Collingridge. Nicolas read the paragraph twice, then a third time, because the idea had the clean, closed shape of something that had been waiting for him.

"Listen to this," he said, and shared his screen. "The Collingridge dilemma. When a technology is new, you can't predict what it'll do. By the time you can see what it does, you can't change it, because it's everywhere."

"Like the software," Frederique said slowly.

"Like the software. Nobody knew it would fail kids in noisy houses when the district signed the contract. Now there's a contract, and a schedule, and everyone's already installed it."

Mika's voice came through steadier than usual. "So it's too early and too late at the same time. That's the worst thing I've ever heard."

"It's kind of elegant," Frederique said. "Horrible and elegant."

Nicolas felt a strange exhilaration, the kind that came with understanding a thing precisely, and then felt embarrassed about feeling it, since the thing understood was the trap they were standing in. He thought of his father's line that rules ossify if you write them too soon, then realized his father had it exactly backwards: the rules weren't the problem. The absence of rules had hardened around a purchase order. He turned that over while Mika argued that they should flood Ms. Sutton's inbox and Frederique argued, more sagacious than anyone their age should have to be, that they should ask for one concrete thing instead of a general grievance, because people could say yes to one thing.

They drafted the statement together, Frederique reading lines aloud, Nicolas typing. They asked that flagged sessions be reviewed by a person before anything went on file, and that the review consider home conditions. They attached the other district's numbers. They did not mention Collingridge, though Nicolas kept the page open in another tab, like a stone in his pocket.

Before they submitted it, Nicolas scrolled back through his own recorded session and found the moment where the circle had pulsed at his raised hand. The software had noted it in a log he hadn't known was public to him: "face partially obscured, 2.1 seconds." He took a screenshot and added it to the attachments. It proved nothing, really. It just showed what the machine counted as worth counting.

He clicked submit at 9:40, and the form returned a gray confirmation box with no warmth in it. Ms. Sutton's reply came the next morning, brief and unmastered: "I'll bring it to the coordinator. No promises. Come by after last period if you want to talk." Nicolas read it twice, then closed the laptop and looked for a while at the yard, where a neighbor's sprinkler turned and turned, watering the same strip of grass it always watered. He put the laptop in his bag for school.

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: Risk compensation is the tendency of people to behave less carefully when a safety measure makes them feel protected, so the measure can deliver less benefit than predicted.
story:
Nolan had signed up for the hospital volunteer program because the application asked what he would do with his summer, and he had wanted an answer better than nothing. On Tuesdays he delivered water pitchers and mail to rooms on the fourth floor, and by the third week the nurses let him take the long cart down to the ER annex without checking on him. It was in the annex, near the end of a shift that had to be finished by six so he could catch the bus, that he saw Brenden come through the sliding doors with his arm wrapped in a dish towel and his new helmet still clipped to his backpack.

"Brenden," Nolan said, steering the cart out of the traffic lane. "What happened?"

"Hill on Mercer. Took the turn fast and the gravel got me." Brenden grinned through what was clearly pain. "Cool helmet, right? Got it Saturday. Full shell, the good foam. I've been hitting forty down that hill since I got it."

Nolan walked with him to the desk and then sat in the plastic chairs while a nurse took Brenden's blood pressure. He kept one eye on the wall clock. His cart still had three trays on it, and the charge nurse had made it clear that nothing went back upstairs after 5:45. He was weighing the trays against the friend when he heard himself say, slowly, like he was finding the idea on the floor, "You got the helmet and then you started riding faster."

"Obviously. That's what it's for. I used to ride that hill like a coward."

Nolan had read something in the pamphlet rack during a slow hour two weeks ago, something that had seemed abstract then, an essay about why safety measures often delivered less than predicted. He turned it over now while Brenden flexed his fingers for the nurse. "It's called risk compensation," he said. "People behave less carefully when a safety measure makes them feel protected, so the measure can deliver less benefit than predicted." The sentence came out flat, like something he had carried in his pocket. "The helmet isn't wrong. The speed is the problem."

From where Brenden sat, the waiting room looked different than it had from the chairs. He watched the clock too, because his mother's shift ended at six and she would find out about the arm before he could frame it, and he watched Nolan stand, torn, one hand still on the cart. He watched him decide. Nolan left the trays by the desk with a scrawled note and stayed through the X-ray, and that surprised Brenden more than the gravel had. He was used to being the one people watched, not the one people stayed for. When the doctor came back with the films, Brenden asked her, quietly, whether a helmet did anything if you were going fast enough, and she said the helmet protected the head, and left the rest of the sentence where it was.

They had twenty minutes to make the bus, and the crepuscular light through the annex windows had gone from gold to gray by the time Brenden got his splint and his discharge papers. Walking out, Brenden said, "So what am I supposed to do, ride slow forever? That's not living." Nolan pushed the empty cart ahead of him and considered the question honestly, because he had been considering a version of it all afternoon. He thought of the pamphlet essay, all clean logic and no blood, and thought that rationalism looked different from a plastic chair in an ER. He did not believe Brenden should be absolved of the speed by blaming the helmet, and he did not believe the helmet was the villain either. Both things were true and neither settled anything.

"You could keep the helmet and lose the forty," Nolan said as they reached the curb. "That's all I've got."

"That's a terrible argument," Brenden said, but he said it while clipping the helmet to the backpack strap where it would be harder to reach, and the bus pulled up before either of them could call it wisdom. On board, Brenden fell asleep against the window with his splinted arm in his lap, and Nolan texted the charge nurse an apology about the trays. She replied that the trays were fine, and that a family on the fourth floor had asked whether the polite water boy would be back Tuesday. Nolan looked up from the screen. Across the aisle, a man who had not been wearing a seatbelt, the nurse had mentioned, was being wheeled toward imaging, and behind the ambulance doors the hill on Mercer waited for nobody in particular.

"Next stop, Mercer Street," the driver called.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: In Schenck v. United States (1919), Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote that free speech would not protect a man falsely shouting fire in a theatre and causing a panic.
story:
The assignment went up on the board in Ms. Abdi's classroom on a Tuesday: each student would argue both sides of a free speech case before a mock Supreme Court, petitioner in the morning, respondent after lunch. Isla had wanted the environmental law unit. She said so, and Ms. Abdi said that the Court had never once asked her opinion on the curriculum, which Isla took to mean no.

She built her restriction side first, because it was easier. She found the quotation on the second page of her research, in three different places, always the same words, always presented as if it had been handed down on a stone tablet: free speech would not protect a man falsely shouting fire in a theatre and causing a panic. It was perfect. It sounded like common sense wearing a robe. She wrote it on an index card and underlined it twice, and when Priya asked what she was so pleased about, Isla read it aloud in the voice she used for imitating their vice principal.

"That's Holmes," Charles-Olivier said from the next row, not looking up from his laptop. "Oliver Wendell Holmes. Schenck, 1919."

"I know it's a real case," Isla said, although until that moment she had not thought about it being a case at all. She had thought of it as weather, as something that simply existed.

"Look up who Schenck was," Charles-Olivier said, and closed the laptop with the small ceremony he reserved for having won something without appearing to compete.

That night Isla found the whole thing. Schenck v. United States, 1919, the opinion written by Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes, who said that free speech would not protect a man falsely shouting fire in a theatre and causing a panic. Charles-Olivier had found it before she did, and had left a message in the class forum at 11:40 p.m., which she read at 11:52.

Isla, since you'll quote this tomorrow anyway: the man who wrote it was Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes, in Schenck v. United States, 1919. Schenck was a socialist pamphleteer. Look up what he was pamphleting about, and then decide whether the fire line is your best weapon or Charles-Olivier's. C.O.

She did look it up, and then she sat for a while with the index card in her hand, feeling the specific embarrassment of having been handed a rhetorical treasure by someone who had never intended to give it away. The quotation was real, and it was powerful, and it had been written to send a man to prison for handing out leaflets. All three of those things were true at once, and none of them cancelled the others out.

In the morning she argued for restriction anyway, but differently. She stood at the podium in the multipurpose room, three rows of eleventh graders arranged as justices, and she told them what Holmes had written and when. "In 1919, in Schenck v. United States, Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote that free speech would not protect a man falsely shouting fire in a theatre and causing a panic," she said. "I'm quoting him against my own side's interests here, so pay attention." She laid out the case for limits, and then she laid out the case's biography, the same sentence used to justify silencing dissent, and she watched Priya, in the justices' row, start writing fast.

At lunch she sat in the stairwell with her notes for the afternoon, arguing the opposite of everything she had argued that morning. The trouble was that she no longer believed either position cleanly. She believed speech could cause real harm, the way a false shout can, and she believed governments had used exactly that argument to lock up people whose only crime was a printing press, and both beliefs sat in her like two tenants sharing a kitchen. She could not make them merge. She could only make them speak to each other.

When the afternoon session began, Charles-Olivier argued the absolutist side as if he had never heard of Schenck, which she suspected was a kind of compliment. On cross-examination she rose and asked him whether a man who falsely shouts fire in a crowded theatre and causes a panic should be prosecuted, and he paused for one second too long, and in that second Priya leaned toward the girl next to her and whispered something that made both of them look at Isla instead of him.

Ms. Abdi gave no verdict, because the ninth-grade justices had deadlocked, four to four, with one abstention on the grounds that he hadn't done the reading. Afterward, in the corridor, Charles-Olivier fell into step beside her.

"So which one do you actually believe?" he asked.

"I'll let you know," Isla said, "around forty."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: The world's first food bank, St. Mary's Food Bank in Phoenix, Arizona, was founded in 1967 by John van Hengel.
story:
Victoria printed the waiver at the kitchen table and signed it while her mother washed dishes, because the food bank's website said volunteers under nineteen needed a parent's signature too, and her mother had signed without reading it, which Victoria decided not to hold against her. Her college application was already submitted. That was the honest part. The volunteering was for the hours her guidance counselor had suggested, though nobody was checking, and she had chosen the Saturday before Thanksgiving mostly because Sameer had said he'd come and then cancelled at eleven the night before with a text that read, family thing, sorry, tell them I said hi.

She drove herself. The warehouse sat behind a church a few neighborhoods over, in a part of town she usually only passed on the way to the river trail, where a brown sign used the word riparian and her junior year biology teacher had made them memorize it anyway, standing on the boardwalk in the rain. The parking lot was already half full when she arrived at eight forty.

Inside, a woman in a lanyard introduced herself as Ms. Becker and handed Victoria a hairnet. "You'll be on sorting," she said. "Canned goods first, then the produce when the truck comes."

The cans came in bins from a weekend food drive at the elementary school. Victoria's job was to check dates and sort by type into labeled flats: soups, vegetables, protein, fruit. Next to her a retired man worked the same line at twice her speed and narrated his opinions about dented cans, and across the table a girl she recognized vaguely from another school peeled labels off jars of peanut butter that had been taped over, for privacy, someone's name written in marker underneath.

On the wall above the sink hung a poster with a timeline of the food bank's history. She read it on her first trip to the handwashing station, because the water took a long time to get hot. The world's first food bank was St. Mary's Food Bank in Phoenix, Arizona, founded in 1967 by John van Hengel. She read the line twice. She had assumed food banks were older, somehow, like libraries, something that had always existed once people thought of it. Sixty years, she calculated, standing there with wet hands. Her grandmother was older than the entire concept.

"Did you know that?" she asked the retired man when she got back to the line. "That this all started in 1967? A guy in Phoenix, John van Hengel."

"Phoenix," he said, holding a can of green beans up to the light. "Hot place to be hungry."

There was a problem at ten. A family came through the client door, which faced the sorting floor, and a boy of maybe seven had a plastic bag and started pulling items from the Thanksgiving display table while his mother filled out paperwork at the front desk. One of the other volunteers, a college-aged guy in a church group shirt, moved toward him and said, gently, "Buddy, that's for after check-in," and the boy put back a box of stuffing but kept his hand on it, and his mother came over fast and said something low to him in Spanish and he took his hand off the box and stood with both hands behind his back like a soldier.

Victoria kept sorting. She sorted through the whole exchange, beans, beans, soup, expired, beans, and found she was working faster, and made herself slow down. She had come here to assuage something, she understood that now, sitting with it for the first time; some vague guilt about applying to schools with forty-thousand-dollar tuition while this boy stood with his hands behind his back. But the sorting itself was not about her guilt. The sorting was soup going in the soup flat. Both things were true at once and she could not make them into one thing.

The truck arrived at eleven and she was sent to help carry boxes of produce, oranges and cabbage and a pallet of sweet potatoes that had been donated by a farm upstate. Sameer texted a photo from his cousin's engagement party, buffet table, him giving a thumbs up, and she sent back a photo of the sweet potatoes. He replied, "jealous," and she believed him about four percent.

At the break, Ms. Becker brought out a plate of day-old donuts and told them that demand went up every November and the number of first-time families went up too, people who had never needed it before and were embarrassed, so smile when they come through the line. It was the closest thing to a speech anyone made all day, and even it was mostly about donuts.

When the family with the boy left, an hour later, they had their bags, and the stuffing was in one of them, and the boy waved at Victoria on the way out, a small sideways wave, not a real one, and she waved back the same way. She had four hours logged. She would come back in December, she had already decided, though she hadn't decided whether to tell Sameer or let him find out by coming himself. She peeled off the hairnet and stood in the parking lot with her keys in her hand.

Her mother texted: how was it. She typed three different answers and deleted them, and then the retired man came out carrying his coat and called across the lot, "See you Saturday?"

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: Freezing food at -18 degrees Celsius (0 degrees Fahrenheit) stops bacteria from growing but does not kill most of them, so thawed food can spoil again.
story:
Nicholas had never planned a meal in his life, unless counting the times he'd opened the cupboard, seen three kinds of crackers, and chosen one. His mother's surgery was scheduled for a Tuesday, his father would be at the hospital, and for the following week Nicholas would be feeding himself. Karan had offered his kitchen on Saturday, saying his own parents worked weekends and the house would be empty except for Mackenna, who was, in Karan's words, "scarily competent."

The grocery store was the first test. Nicholas had a list he'd drafted from a website Karan had sent him, and the list kept failing. It called for one onion as though onions were sold that way, and it assumed he knew the difference between the two kinds of soy sauce. Mackenna steered the cart and let him make his own mistakes, intervening only twice: once to move a bag of frozen shrimp back to the freezer aisle after he'd left it in the cereal section, and once to point out that buying a whole chicken when no one in his house would carve it was a decision made by a person who wanted to feel capable rather than a person who wanted dinner.

"You're buying ingredients for a week," she said. "Not for a personality."

Back at Karan's house, the plan was four dishes cooked in one afternoon: a pot of chili, a tray of baked pasta with enough sauce to freeze separately, a soup, and a batch of rice that would go into the freezer in flat bags so it wouldn't turn into a brick. Karan's kitchen was larger than Nicholas's and better equipped, and Karan himself drifted in and out, eating slices of the cheese that was supposed to go on the pasta and offering commentary. When Nicholas burned the first batch of garlic, Karan delivered a small speech about how cooking shows lionized chefs who tossed everything in a pan over high heat, when the truth was that most food wanted to be left alone. Nicholas started the garlic again on the lowest flame, and it turned pale gold without turning bitter, which felt like a fact he'd discovered rather than been taught.

The chili came together by mid-afternoon. Nicholas tasted it, added cumin, tasted again, and wrote the amounts on the back of the receipt so he could repeat it. Ms. Takahashi, Karan's neighbour, knocked on the door around four to return a ladder, and stayed long enough to look at the stove and ask what they were making. She ate a spoonful of the soup, said "more salt, and don't be shy about it," and left. Her verdict seemed more valuable than anything on the website, because she'd actually eaten it.

Then the argument started, and it was about the freezer. Karan wanted to put the leftover soup from last weekend, a container that had been sitting in the fridge for six days, into the freezer so it would keep for later. Nicholas thought this was fine, since freezing, as far as he understood it, made food safe. Mackenna set down the knife she'd been using and disagreed.

"Freezing at minus eighteen stops bacteria from growing," she said. "It doesn't kill most of them. Thawed food can spoil again."

"So they're just asleep," Karan said.

"They're waiting. Whatever was in that soup on Thursday is still in it. You put it in the freezer, you take it out in a month, and you're back where you started, except now you trust it because it was frozen."

Nicholas looked at the container. The soup inside had a skin on the surface and he had been half avoiding the question of whether he'd have eaten it. He carried it to the compost bin under the sink and scraped it out, and the sound it made was wet and unappetizing, and that settled something in him more thoroughly than Mackenna's explanation had. He was aware, though, that he'd taken her word for it. He hadn't checked. She was the kind of person other people believed without checking, and that was exactly the problem.

Later, while the pasta baked and the kitchen windows fogged, Nicholas sat at the counter with his phone and looked it up himself. She was right about the number, right about the growing versus the killing, and right about thawed food spoiling again. He also found opinions about how long things kept, and those opinions disagreed with each other, and none of them addressed the actual question he had, which was whether the chili he'd made today would be good on Thursday or merely safe. He read for a while and then stopped, because he noticed he was trying to replace one authority with another, and the whole point of the afternoon had been that he was going to learn to feed himself, which included deciding when a smell was wrong.

They portioned everything into labelled bags. Nicholas wrote the dates with a marker Mackenna produced from a drawer, and he wrote them in a format he'd chosen himself, day first then month, so his future self would not have to guess. Karan claimed two portions of chili as payment for use of the kitchen. Ms. Takahashi's ladder stood by the door still, apparently forgotten, and Karan said he'd return it tomorrow.

Nicholas walked home at dusk carrying one bag of rice and one bag of chili in a backpack, along with the receipt with the chili recipe on the back. At home he cleared a shelf in the freezer, moving the bag of forgotten peas and the half-loaf of bread to make room, and set the flat bags inside. The chili, dated today, went in last. He stood with the freezer door open for a moment, looking at the small organized shelf, then closed it and went to wash the dishes.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: In the seeding method, chopped chocolate that is already tempered is stirred into melted chocolate to supply form V crystals for the rest to copy.
story:
Hunter arrived at the community kitchen on Delmore Street with a paper bag of chopped chocolate and a suspicion that he was about to waste an entire afternoon. Mr. Vargas had put a sign-up sheet on the door in April: Saturday sessions, learn something with your hands, no experience required. Courtney had written her name first and then Hunter's, in that order, without asking him, which he had decided not to treat as an indictment of his initiative.

The room smelled of onions from the morning soup shift, though the burners had been wiped down and the big steel counters cleared. Mr. Vargas set out thermometers, silicone spatulas, bowls, and one marble slab the size of a cafeteria tray, which he carried like something sleeping. "Chocolate is the most honest ingredient in this building," he said. "It tells you exactly what you did wrong. You just have to know how to read it." Then, as promised on the sheet, he stopped instructing and stood by the sink drinking coffee, leaving them to the melting pot and the recipe card.

Hunter chopped a bar into uneven rubble while Courtney read the card aloud, her finger moving under each line. Melt, cool on the slab, work it with the spatula until it thickens, warm it back gently. The first batch went wrong in a way Hunter found almost interesting: the chocolate set dull and streaked, and when he pressed a corner it bent like an eraser instead of snapping. He kept the failed square on the counter as evidence, as if it might eventually confess.

"You're staring at it like it's going to apologize," Courtney said.

"I'm staring at it because something happened in there and I want to know what." He turned the square over. The underside had a faint bloom, pale gray, like frost that had changed its mind. He wondered whether the chocolate had chosen that pattern or been forced into it, and whether there was any difference between those two things at the scale of crystals. He didn't say that out loud. He said, "Again."

The second attempt also failed, though differently, which Hunter logged silently as a kind of progress. Between tries, Nickolas showed up, an hour late, carrying a grocery bag and wearing the expression of someone who had already rehearsed his excuse. His father's restaurant had taken the marble slabs to the new location, he said, and his father had also taken the good thermometer, and anyway he had a batch he had to finish today for his sister's engagement party, and could he please just work beside them.

"You don't need a slab if you already have tempered chocolate," Hunter said, mostly to himself. He was rereading the recipe card, and the phrase seed chocolate had snagged on something. He looked at Nickolas's grocery bag, at the two bars of store-bought chocolate sticking out of it, chocolate he happened to know Nickolas had bought because the wrapper advertised a snap. He picked one up and snapped a corner off against the counter. Clean. Bright. Almost musical.

"It's already tempered," Hunter said. "That's what seed means, I think." He took the bowl of melted chocolate, still warm, and began stirring in the chopped pieces a handful at a time, watching them dissolve slower than he expected, watching the gloss on the surface change by degrees he couldn't name. "Chopped chocolate that's already tempered gets stirred into melted chocolate, and the melted part copies it." He said it carefully, testing the sentence the way you'd test a plank across a stream. Courtney leaned in and asked how the melted chocolate knew what to copy, and Hunter admitted he didn't know, only that it did, and that this bothered him pleasantly, the way a locked door in your own house does.

Nickolas stood beside him with his phone showing a video of someone doing the same thing, and for a while the three of them worked in a row, auxiliary to one another, one stirring, one holding the thermometer, one timing. When Nickolas's batch reached temperature, they spread it thin on parchment and waited. The kitchen clock ticked through four minutes. Mr. Vargas drifted over, coffee in hand, and looked down at the setting chocolate without touching it.

Hunter broke off a shard and held it up to the window. It shone. He bent it over the counter and it snapped, a real snap, clean-edged, and he felt something in his chest go quiet and satisfied at once. He still had his own two failed squares lined up like suspects, and he still didn't fully understand what had gone wrong with them, or why the seed method had worked when the slab method hadn't, or whether the difference was in him or in the chocolate.

"So I can do this at home without buying marble," Nickolas said, rewrapping his second bar.

"Apparently you just have to buy chocolate that already knows how to be chocolate." Hunter set the shard down next to the dull squares, shiny beside streaky, and took a photo of both. "Send me the rest of that bar," he said. "I want to try again before I believe it."

fact: Mexico's Day of the Dead is traditionally celebrated on November 1 and 2, when families build ofrendas, or home altars, with photos and the favorite foods and drinks of relatives who have died.
story:
The kitchen smelled of cinnamon and warm dough, and the sweet bread was cooling on the rack where her grandmother's teapot used to sit. Emma's mother had been up since five, and now, at two in the afternoon, relatives would start arriving by four, which left Emma with a folding table, a purple cloth, and the problem of what belonged on it.

"Abuela died in March," her mother said, smoothing the cloth. "So this year we do it properly. You build it, Emma. You're the one with the time." Then she went back to the kitchen, because the tamales would not wait and neither would the aunts.

Emma stood alone in the living room with the phone pressed to her ear. Aurelie had come over the night before, half to help and half to escape her own house, and now she was on speaker from her car. "I looked it up after I left," Aurelie said. "The whole thing has a name. It's called an ofrenda. You put it up on the first and second of November, Day of the Dead, and the photos and the food and the drinks you set out are supposed to be the favorites of the person who died. Not what looks nice. What she actually liked."

"Then we're already wrong," Emma said. Her mother had bought the pan dulce from the Mexican bakery on Aldine, the round one with the sugar crust, because the woman there said it was traditional. Emma had a photo, a small one from 1994, but she wasn't sure what her grandmother had actually eaten.

The doorbell rang at three, earlier than the aunts. It was Harman, holding a grocery bag. He had lived across the street since Emma was nine, and he had cut the grandmother's lawn for money all through high school, which had turned into not-quite-money, into coffee on her porch and her acerbic opinions about his college applications. "I know I'm early," he said. "But I kept thinking about it. I brought tequila, because she told me once she drank it at her sister's wedding in 1971 and never again. That's a favorite, isn't it? Once counts."

Emma took the bottle. It was heavy in her hand, and the decision in front of her felt heavier. Her mother's version of the altar was the traditional one, the one the bakery woman described, sweet bread and marigolds and the photo in the center. But her grandmother had been a woman who told the priest he talked too fast, who kept a jar of pickles fermenting on the back porch until the neighbors complained, who had opinions about everything being done correctly and no patience for things done only for show.

Harman set the tequila on the table and unwrapped the bread, tearing the heel off and eating it while Emma held the photo. Aurelie's voice came tinny from the phone on the windowsill: "Favorites, not decorations. That's the whole rule." Her mother appeared in the doorway with a pot holder still on her hand, saw the tequila, and paused. Emma expected her to object. Instead she said, "Put it near the front. She'd want people to see it and ask."

They built it together in the last hour. Emma placed the photo where the light from the window crossed it, and the tequila beside it, and the sweet bread, and then, after a moment, the jar of pickle brine Harman fetched from the porch railing where the family had left it out of grief or superstition or neither. Her mother added the coffee cup with the chipped rim, the grandmother's actual cup, unwashed since March, which made Emma's throat close. Harman folded paper marigolds from a video because the flower shop had sold out, and Aurelie stayed on the phone the whole time, describing where the sugar skulls should go, as if distance had made her the altar's acolyte.

When the aunts arrived they circled the table, and the youngest one picked up the tequila and laughed, a sudden wet laugh, and said, "She did drink it, at Rosa's wedding, and Papa didn't speak to her for a week." Then everyone was talking at once, and Emma stood back and looked at what they had made. It was her mother's tradition and her grandmother's stubbornness set side by side, and she could not have said which part mattered more, or whether the dead could taste any of it, or whether that was even the question. The candles were lit as the sky went dark, and Harman handed her the last piece of sweet bread, the heel, still warm where he had held it.
